en: Preface to the Carved Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* by Zhiyi.
The volumes of the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* commentary are vast and extensive, nearly rivalling those of the three [other] divisions.
Each division has its own record (*ji*) by Jingxi [Zhanran], much like the *Zhengyi* commentaries on the Five Classics. However, as for the literary style of these records, the three divisions...

The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) is concise, whereas [the present work] is extensive. Although both are commentaries on a major scripture, there is a specific reason why one record is more detailed than the other.
All three sections were expounded over the course of ninety days; what was recorded by Zhizhe (Zhang’an) had to be concise.
However, for the meaning to be fully revealed, the commentary must provide a thorough and exhaustive explanation—this is the reason for this extensive exposition. As for the *Jing*... [text ends].
It is called the *Shu* (Commentary). The Great Master personally ordered his attendants to record it; therefore, its text is extensive and its meaning complete.
As for the *Ji* (Record), it merely provides annotations and explanations for difficult passages and essential meanings, which is sufficient. This is why it is a concise commentary.

Although the extensive and concise versions differ, in their precise selection of the doctrinal gates (*jiaomen*) and their clarification of the path of contemplation (*guandao*) to support and aid the fundamental tenets, they are not at all unequal.
This is consistent with my own previous commentary on the *Śāstra*. I have long perceived the subtle understanding and skillful explanations contained in this record;
however, as the entire work had long been lost and scattered, I was unable to view it again, seeing only a fragmentary glimpse through broken passages and surviving fragments.

Recently, Hyanghwon Chijū (Ciyuan) of Kyeju Temple specifically sought it out at the Kōfuku-ji in Nanto, and indeed recovered the complete manuscript to bring back. Upon seeing it, Master Ryonggong [was deeply moved].

He was delighted and consequently requested that I participate in the editorial collation for its publication. However, as I happened to be burdened by illness and a heavy accumulation of affairs, I was unable to attend to the task.

I therefore entrusted it to Master Nanxi Baizhi Qiu. Master Qiu then undertook the collation and ordered the carving of the blocks, so that the work may now be presented to the world in its entirety, flawless and radiant.
This is truly a magnificent achievement. If students rely on this record to investigate and study the *Shu-wen*, and rely on this *Shu-wen*...
If one seeks the meaning of the scriptural text, then this inconceivable liberation can be realized immediately.
One breathes through the same nostril as the Elder Mahākāśyapa in the city of Vaiśālī. Thus, I have written these few words at the beginning of the scroll as a preface.

On the full moon day of the second month of winter in the year of Wumǔ (1758) of the Genbun era, this *Commentary on the Discerning Words of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra Sub-commentary* was respectfully composed and engraved by the śramaṇa Ryōjun of Tiantai Mountain, Dongxi.
The commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* by the Wise One contains profound meanings and deep purports;
it is vast and great! Thus, for scholars to fathom it is truly difficult. Yet this difficulty does not lie elsewhere but within oneself; it does not lie afar but nearby.
Is it truly difficult? Or is it truly not difficult? If one wishes to know why it is truly difficult, yet attain its realization—[it lies in the self].
That which was previously not difficult for me to obtain—this record of Shapingling—I have now followed its path. Alas, the complete manuscript had been lost and dispersed;

what remained in circulation were merely fragmentary chapters and incomplete volumes. Was it perhaps because Heaven had not yet wished to destroy this culture that I was able to behold the complete set once again?
This was truly the time [for such a recovery]. (Qingqiu) mistakenly bears the responsibility for correcting errors; it is also the time [to fulfill that duty].

I did not collate and edit it for circulation; however, as this book was merely transcribed within our own country, there are many errors and doubts, and no second copy exists against which to verify them.
How could one of shallow learning and dull wit dare to undertake such a task? Nevertheless, to strive for it even with forced effort is still better than doing nothing at all.
Since it was possible to do so and yet I could not refrain, I have accordingly sought out the surviving fragments of various editions circulating in the world and...

In the *Yujì* (Record of Yu), I have cited and compared various editions, cross-referencing and collating them numerous times. Having gradually reached a degree of certainty, I have applied lead and yellow pigment to designate those parts for carving into woodblocks.

Among these, there remain instances that are ambiguous or differ by a mere fraction of a *shēng*; these I have marked at the top [of the page] but did not dare to alter arbitrarily. As for those that are entirely correct, I have marked every detail, both large and small. As for those that are entirely erroneous, I have generally... *(Note:

The original text appears to be an excerpt from a preface or colophon concerning textual criticism and the preparation of a printed edition. The final sentence is truncated, but the intent is clear: the author has meticulously identified and corrected errors while preserving uncertain readings.)*

If one does not adopt that which is ambiguous and difficult to adjudicate, then one should instead present it so that [the student] may discern the differences and similarities; let the reader examine this.
Alas! This record serves as an exposition to enable scholars to know that words and liberation can be approached and yet not approached, and can be distanced from and yet reached through.
Thus, the lamp and the oil assist one another in the essence of the commentaries on the sutras, and through their mutual application, they reach realization.
If one does not immediately transcend the partiality of "discussing food" and "counting jewels," one does not immediately reach the immediate;

if one does not immediately transcend the madness of dark realization and lack of learning, one does not immediately reach the immediate. This is the subtlety of mutually rescuing from the two maladies of neither-attaining-nor-abandoning.

Otherwise, how difficult it is to fathom its true reality! If one does not rely on scriptural explanations, then either one falls into partiality or one falls into madness; if one is not mad, then one is partial. Thus, one must fathom it.
Is it not difficult to fathom its reality? How magnificent is this record! It remedies defects, corrects partiality, and serves as wings for this Way.
This is surely the constant practice of our school in studying the teachings; were it otherwise, it would not be so. The purport of this record lies specifically here:

who would find it difficult to know the constant? Yet the words concerning the constant are what is difficult at the end. What is difficult at the end? Only this is difficult. It is not that one lacks the knowledge.

The words "constant" and "difficult" are hard to realize in the heart. Those who rely on written records for understanding ultimately cause what is difficult to remain difficult, unaware that it is not difficult because it is close at hand within themselves. Thus, one must examine whether it is truly difficult or truly not difficult.
Preface to the Commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, respectfully composed by the śramaṇa Qingqiu Miaocheng of the Baoji Jiaoyuan on South Creek at Mount Tiantai,
on the first day of the twelfth month of the Ding-si year of the Yuanwen era.
To begin with, when the Three Powers first differentiated, the One Qi was generated above the Way; when the three springs were nearly returning, the One Yang restored itself within the earth.
As the three axes were about to move, one scroll appeared beneath the ritual altar; this is the natural numerical order of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
Indeed, when Jingxi composed his *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, it consisted of three scrolls of vast breadth.
It is fully endowed with the three truths, the three contemplations, and the three thousand worlds.
The teachings of a single lifetime and the eighty-four thousand dharma-treasuries are all contained within one nature, one mind, and one thought-moment.

With the contemplation of the mind as the warp and all dharmas as the woof, they are woven into a fabric that is unlike any other; this is what is meant by "vast" and "great," which is beyond description.

Having obtained [these texts], I have reflected upon them. I have examined various books; some commentaries (*shu*) are extensive while others are concise, each following its own specific purpose and the preferences of its author.

Some records (*ji*) are numerous while others are few, likely due to later generations having divided the volumes. The *Tonghui sengzhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks with Comprehensive Wisdom) lists a concise version of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-ṭīkā* in ten fascicles and a record of that commentary (*Vimalakīrti-ṭīkā-jì*) in three fascicles.
Although these do not explicitly state they are "extensive," they stand in contrast to the "concise" versions mentioned above.

The *Zhi Guang* (Broad Commentary) was thus produced from the *Gu Shan Chui Yu Xu* (Preface by Gu Shan on the Transmission of Kindness) in thirty-four fascicles and the *Ji* (Record) in three fascicles;

this is the origin of the *Shu Guang Ji Lue* (Broad Record of the Commentary, Abridged). When later students rely upon the *Guang*, *Shu*, and *Ji* to investigate the text and meaning of the *Lue Shu* (Abridged Commentary), they find them to be mutually interwoven.

The *Ci Yun Han Lu* (Catalogue of Ci Yun’s Collection) lists ten fascicles of the *Lue Shu* and six fascicles of the *Guang Shu Ji*; it concludes by stating that the *Ji* corresponds to the *Guang Shu*.

The scriptural phrasing differs slightly, yet the interpretation perfectly accords [with the original]. According to the *Donghu Tongji* and the *Jingxi Benji*, the *Lüeshu* (Brief Commentary) consists of ten fascicles and the *Ji* (Record) consists of three fascicles;
the *Guangshu* (Extensive Commentary) and its *Ji* consist of six fascicles. While the three-fascicle version appears to be the *Lüeshu Ji*, it is not recorded in the *Shanjia Jiaodian Zhi*.
Conversely, the three-fascicle version cites the *Guangshu Ji* of six fascicles and records it therein, whereas the *Zhi* does not.
Why do you reflect upon this? Although the *Jueji* (Record of Decisions) by Zhenzhong of Eizan does not include it in its enumeration, its compiler states:

"The *Miaole ji* (Commentary on the Wondrous Joy) explains the *Xiangguang shu* (Extensive Commentary), and the *Daoshen ji* (Commentary by Daoshen) explains the *Lüeshu* (Abridged Commentary). Judging from this, it is clear that Jingxi did not record the *Lüeshu*.

As for its inclusion in the enumeration, it is merely a matter of different ways of opening and closing [the categories]; why then do you harbor such doubt? It is as if one were saying it is "inclusive."
The Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) are doubled, thus making six; these six are none other than the Way of the Three Powers.
Furthermore, as a single month is divided into its bright and dark phases, the three months of spring likewise constitute the number six. Indeed, the single mind is the totality of all dharmas;
when divided, it becomes the Three Studies of Precept, Concentration, and Wisdom, and when further expanded, it becomes the Six Perfections such as Dāna and so forth. This is the true meaning.
The Record of the Vimalakīrti Hall, composed by the Abbot, states: "Without passing through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one suddenly fulfills the practice of a *sattva*;
without exceeding a single thought-moment, one directly advances toward the fruit of Vairocana. The three bodies are ultimately perfected, for there is nothing superior to this.

This is because purity is the True Body (*dharmakāya*), name is the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the True is the principle realized, and the Responsive is the body manifested—all are of one essence."
The three bodies are sometimes divided into six—wisdom, principle, self, other, superior, and inferior—or at times each individual character manifests as a golden grain of Buddha.

Is this enumeration recorded here not marvelous? My humble servant, Kōken, has examined the *Tendai Kōsho* (Extensive Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) brought from China by the Venerable Ganjin; it was transcribed at Nankin by the Great Master Saichō of Tōdai-ji.

He sought further instruction from the Great Tang and transmitted the records of Jingxi; he subsequently commanded that the teachings be established in our own dynasty to be enshrined within the treasury of Ruie Peak.
Thus, Ciyun remarked: "During the Tang era, there was a Japanese monk named Saichō (Jisshō) who took many volumes of the teachings and returned to his country.
Alas, it is regrettable that these various expositions can no longer be heard today. How lamentable! The teachings have their periods of decline and flourishing, and the scriptures have their...

The appearance and disappearance [of this work] is not unique to China; the same is true for Japan. For many years, the extensive commentary (*guǎngshū*) and the sub-commentary (*jì*) have remained hidden from the world.
This summer, while dusting old volumes in the Yingxue Hall, I happened to uncover this opening chapter from within a moth-eaten manuscript beneath a bookshelf.
Unable to contain my joy, I immediately conceived the idea of carving it into printing blocks to share with fellow enthusiasts. It is now that I have finally obtained the text.
A merchant leader arrived carrying an old manuscript and said to me: "I have a vow to carve this *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* commentary.
I have sought it across various monasteries without success; I recently inquired at the Chan gate north of Luo, where it was obtained as effortlessly as a pivot fitting into its socket.
Although the scroll is incomplete, I shall have it carved in wood and circulated, serving as a single stroke to strike forth the rare resonance for future generations."

I hope to receive instruction from the Japanese master and collate this work together. Having heard of this, I opened the volume and read from the "Bodhisattva Chapter" onward, noting my reflections as I went.
The Dharma-gate of the inherent nature (*xingju*) is as radiant as the great sun shining in the sky. Placing the book upon my desk, I remarked:
"As for carving characters into wood, nothing is better than the catalpa tree (*zhǐ*); because it is the longest-lived among all trees, the catalpa is the king of woods," as Dong Zhongshu said.
Regarding what is called the creation of characters by the ancients: that which consists of three strokes with one running through their center is called "Wang" (King).
The three strokes represent Heaven, Earth, and Humanity; connecting them in the center signifies the unification of their Way.

For this reason, our Mountain King Myōjin is called "Myō" (Bright/Manifest); "Myō" represents the identity of the Three Truths as One. As for the character "San" (Mountain), its three vertical strokes—
The single horizontal stroke in the character for "emptiness" (kōng) signifies "one"; the three horizontal strokes in the character for "king" (wáng) signify the Three Truths;

and the single vertical stroke signifies "one" again. Because the two characters [for "king"] contain three strokes that embody the image of the "One Thread" (yìguàn), I have established them as my title.

The same applies to "one mind and three contemplations" (yīxīn sānguān) and "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" (yīniàn sānqiān). For this reason, I protect and uphold the Tiantai [teachings].

"Regarding the teaching that the Emperor protects and covers the state, and so forth—Master Boyang further spoke of the Way giving birth to One, One giving birth to Two, and Two giving birth to Three;
this is an inevitable principle. I have preserved this record in one fascicle, and now two sages have been born;

the words [of the sages] truly have their evidence. Having added punctuation and collated them both, they are presented to you. In another day, they shall surely become three complete volumes, flowing in succession."

The merchant leader, having spread [the text] throughout the world, departed with great joy. From that time forward, as he continued to punctuate and collate it, he occasionally compared it with the commentary from Guanzhong;

only then did he realize that Fang’s [exegesis] matches the principle of the square and that [his own] matches the principle of the circle—how could their relative merits be spoken of as being on the same day?
Did not the Great Master Zhiyi say: "If one examines the commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* by Kumārajīva and Sengzhao, they both employ the same comprehensive approach"?
I have observed that the various Dharma masters of the Liang dynasty who lectured on the text of this sutra all interpreted it according to the perspective of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
How could the words of the Sage Master be anything other than true? Therefore, Baoyun and Daowei remarked:

"The four commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* were already difficult to trust as they used personal views to annotate the Buddha’s scriptures; how much more so is this the case now? This is indeed profound.
That which may be taken as trustworthy and relied upon is the commentary by the Great Dhyāna Master [Jizang], a man of wisdom. Yue Boting also said:

"The commentaries on the sutras by Kumārajīva and Sengzhao mostly adhere to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). While they attain the skillful means (*upāya*) of the provisional meaning, they lose the reality of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*).
If one loses the reality, then both the provisional and the real are non-existent. These words are indeed ultimate! As I look back with longing upon those who possessed [this insight]...
When Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty was still a hidden dragon [before ascending the throne], he requested that Master Zhiyi provide a commentary on Kumārajīva’s *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
After the Great Master passed away, the Emperor offered incantations and prayers over the draft commentary and experienced a dream in which he gained insight into the purport of the commentary.

Consequently, upon his accession as the Crown Prince, he issued an edict for the two masters Huiri and Daoshuang at Daochang Monastery to lecture on the *Vimalakīrti* within the Eastern Palace; however, they did not rely on the commentary and failed to grasp its full significance.

Using the commentaries of the Grand Councilor (Yuanzhao) to adjudicate and explain the scriptural text, the Crown Prince listened to them and took them as his essential core. He propagated them throughout the realm.

Naturally gifted with sagely wisdom, how profound and lucid he was! Furthermore, the Sixth Patriarch of the Avataṃsaka, the Great Master Qingliang, possessed an innate nature and superior intelligence;
he could take up two brushes simultaneously and read nine lines at once. He studied [this work] in the tenth year of the Dali era.
He studied the commentaries on the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* under Master Jingxi.

He served as the gate-teacher for seven emperors throughout nine successive reigns of the Tang dynasty. His completed commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* employs the Tiantai system of doctrinal classification (*jiaoxiang*), as well as the principles of the three contemplations, the three virtues, the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment," and the inherent goodness and inherent evil of nature; was this not most appropriate? Thus, the Emperor...
The *Epitaph for Dharma Master Guting of the Avataṃsaka* composed by Song Lian of the Ming Dynasty states: "The Great Being of Qingliang took no fixed teacher in his studies;
he practiced the commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts. Regarding the learning of Jingxi and Xianshou, he held the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as supreme.

As for the principles of the inherent goodness and inherent evil of nature, the three contemplations and three virtues of Tiantai, and the text concerning the 'three thousand worlds in a single thought'—how could these ever have been [otherwise]?"

If one does not even cite [the teachings] to show them to others, how much more so for the commentaries on the *Mohe zhiguan*, which detail the sequence of cultivation through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?

Indeed, nothing lies outside this reality. It was solely because our ancestor, the Great Master Zhiyi, provided such wondrous discourses on the practice and realization of the "three thousand dharma-natures as inherently evil" (*sānqiān xìng è*) that he could challenge and refute the hundred schools of thought and stand alone preeminent throughout two dynasties. Nevertheless, these are like the "bright spring" and the "pure snow"—[sublime yet difficult to appreciate].
The meaning of the phrase "those who sing high notes have few who harmonize" remains true; although commentaries exist, they lie hidden and are not practiced, which I deeply regret.

Nowadays, those who lecture and explain the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* are numerous. When ascending the seat and grasping the whisk, their eloquence flows like a river and flashes like lightning as they discuss the profound and expound the wondrous.

Yet, they do no more than convey the general intent of Kumārajīva and Sengzhao; how could they know that the present school possesses a perfect and complete realization? Have you not seen what Master Wujinding said regarding Master Sengzhao’s *Guan Tan* (Discourse on Contemplation)?
Even if one is virtuous, if one does not clearly understand that nature is inherently complete (*xingju*), there is a danger of having words without substance.

If even Master Zhaolun, with his sagely wisdom, was still like this, how much more so for those of shallow understanding in these latter days? Therefore, Jingxi said: "If one has not yet even heard the name 'inherent evil in nature' (*xing'e*), how can one believe in the practice of inherent virtues (*xingde*)?
If one does not know that in Tiantai’s teaching, inherent evil is all-pervasive and harmonious, and that the realm of demons is itself quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*)."

To thus recklessly proclaim the Buddha’s principle—that afflictions are themselves awakening and birth-and-death are themselves nirvana—is not only to incur the reproach of being like a mouse squeaking or a bird crying out in the void, but it is also to become a firm object of harassment for the hosts of Māras and various heterodox paths;
alas, how truly fearsome this is! Once the draft was completed, I sent it to a bookshop and had it set down in writing.

Having transcribed this pure text and prepared it for carving on wooden blocks, I was repeatedly requested by others—whose faith had been stirred—to provide a preface to place at the beginning of the work.
Thus, wiping my aged eyes and brushing away the frost from my inkstone, I have composed this brief account to clarify the origins and vicissitudes of this record.
In the year of the Dragon (1700) of the Genroku era, during the month when the *lǜ* corresponds to *huángzhōng* and the fourteenth day of the moon,
the śramaṇa Xiùyún recorded this at his hermitage, the Huíxuǐ Xītǎ Dōngxī Yíngxuě Xuān, on Mount Ruì.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll One.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Tiantái.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Scroll One.

Regarding the explanation of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, the section on "Inexhaustibility" is divided into three parts: first, the formal clarification of inexhaustibility; second, the explanation of the reason for its inexhaustibility;
and third, a detailed analysis through questions and answers. The first part is further divided into two sections: first, citing the five headings from ancient and modern texts;

second, the formal demonstration of the textual locations where "inexhaustibility" is indicated (the reader may consult ancient editions to supplement their understanding of the new version). As for the phrase "immeasurable earnestness," there are generally...

There are two reasons for this intention: first, because at that time the Buddha’s words were numerous; second, because it describes a state that cannot be fully exhausted, such as when worldly people speak of "the immeasurable" or "the endless.
Thus we know that Mañjuśrī briefly proclaimed the Buddha’s intent without resorting to further elaboration;
that he was capable of upholding the Buddha’s intent is indeed for a good reason. The term *yuan* (爰) means "at," "in," or "thereupon"; *yuan zhi* (爰至) simply means "reaching" or "arriving at."
Regarding "Zhendan" (China), according to the *Zhi guan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation), this refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.

As for the phrase "equal in all directions," this clarifies that it pertains to the common division (*sāmānya-varga*) and is not related to the common teaching (*sāmānya-dharma*). Thus, these two "commons" are both shared with the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
[The passage mentions] the *Uvāyi* (Upāsikā) from the *Old Avataṃsaka*. From "beginning with the Pure Land" to "ending with the Dharma-offering": as for the term "Pure Land," it refers to the Buddha.

Master Zhaoshi of the Guo-pin [chapter] maintains that because the Dharma-offerings of the Pure Land all belong to the orthodox teaching (zhengzong), it is sufficient to crown them with this single principle of "the inconceivable" within the orthodox teaching.
Nevertheless, since the various chapters differ, they cannot be without distinct purports;
for instance, when contemplating sentient beings and the Buddha-way as non-dual, how could there not be different paths? As already refuted in the commentary, this opens up the peripheral scriptures.

The meaning of "the *kō* (sections) and so forth" is that [this teaching] differs from both masters because it intends to transcend them; it differs from other Chan masters because it is based on the scriptures;

and it differs from other Dharma masters because it does not cling to fixed interpretations. Now, as for the Buddha’s teaching being "exhaustively complete," this is because the five periods differ according to the varying capacities of sentient beings;
thus they are called "distinctive sources. A source is the initial springing forth of water, used as a metaphor for the beginning of the response to capacities. Although there are five periods...
Because there would be no fault of missing the opportunity to act, one attains a virtuous beginning and end; this possesses three meanings.

Since the "Preface" (序) is fundamentally the sequence for the "Correct Transmission" (正流通), which pertains to the "Correct Doctrine" (正宗), these three must not be deficient; therefore, it is said to be "complete.

Regarding the statement that "one must first manifest auspicious omens to signify the manifestation [of the teaching]," the question is: why is the Preface not described as the "Manifestation" (表發)? Why is the Preface used as the Manifestation, while the Manifestation itself is treated separately?
Question: Does the "Preface" (xu) describe the manifestation of auspicious omens? Answer: The preface describes only the manifestation of auspicious omens and the two reasons;
therefore, it is not necessary. Question: If that is so, why is there a descriptive preface at the beginning of the sutra? Answer: What fault would there be in its absence?

Furthermore, there are sutras that lack a descriptive preface, such as those wishing to expound the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and others; because the *Prajñā* is illumination, light serves as its symbolic representation.
The reason why that sutra repeatedly emits light is because it uses the emission of light—as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—to symbolize the "Middle.

Since all three sections of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* are "middle," and as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* uses constant light to symbolize the "Constant" (where all three are simultaneously constant), we know that the present sutra manifests the land to symbolize the "Land" (where all three are simultaneously the Buddha-land). This profound principle is clearly evident throughout the various teachings. If this is so...

Question: Why does the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* not take the "Middle" as its primary tenet? Answer: Because when one adopts the perspective of the identity of principle, there is nothing that is not the One Vehicle;

thus, those capable of hearing the Sage’s intent [are all included]. Therefore, it should be known that the manifestation of auspicious omens serves as the catalyst for the arising of the name [of this sūtra] through the conditions of sentient beings' faculties;

there is indeed a profound reason for this. It is also like the disparagement of the Small and the exhortation toward the Great: although these occurred in the past and were not themselves auspicious omens, they likewise represent the present sūtra.

Auspicious omens have manifested in advance to assist in the accomplishment of this present undertaking; since its purpose accords with the Correct Principle (*saddharma*), it is appropriate to present it first.

Regarding "without stagnation or obstruction": stagnation refers to internal impediments, while obstruction refers to external hindrances. Reaching down to the final age of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), there are none who are not moistened by its grace;

thus, there is no stagnation or obstruction whatsoever. As for "the Tathāgata’s power assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation": this begins from the time of human beings and continues until the period when [the teachings] have not yet been formally sealed or established.
Regarding "establishing as a perfected one," the Dharma can be certified; how could it be that a person who has certified the True Sūtra is not certified as a Master of Transformation?

As for "the mind and mind being quiescent," this follows the literal meaning of the name to accord with the principle; the same applies to the circulation of the *Guanmen* (Contemplation Gate). Therefore, I have formulated this interpretation.

Regarding "arising and ceasing," this refers to the meaning at the beginning and end of the chapter, as divided in the text into two: the Preface and the Main Body. Within the Main Body, there are the outer and inner sections, which emerge [from the text].

The "Chamber" (the introductory section) and the "Leaving the Chamber" (the main body) further distinguish the emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Regarding the *Ratnakūṭa-paripṛcchā* concerning the causes and conditions of the Buddha-land:
"I wish to hear how one attains the purity of the Buddha-land" asks about the fruit; "I only pray that you will explain the practice for the Pure Land" asks about the cause.

These are explained collectively because they have not yet been divided into four parts; therein, there are five sections: first, clarifying the purpose of the coming [of the teaching]; second, from "That which is spoken... onwards, the Buddha... [and so forth].
1. The country is named "Three" (Traya); 2. It is also called "Below," which sets forth its alternative names; 3. "The Buddha-land" below distinguishes between phenomena and principle;
4. "Or perhaps" below refutes the meaning of the four [extreme] natures. Regarding the initial intent: although the text has not yet appeared, the meaning is already complete;

now we merely reiterate its essential purport. Regarding the distinction between phenomena and principle: "Eternal Quiescence" belongs to principle, while the remaining three reside in phenomena. If...
It merely states that the two bodies should both be called "Responsive" (*nirmāṇakāya*); this is the next point, which first provides a brief summary.

Then, under the heading "Ultimate Principle," it clarifies the reasons why there is a phenomenal realm; and under "Not Original," it clarifies the mutual relation between phenomenon and principle, as well as their mutual identity. Regarding the fact that lands exist without a cause:

although the calculation [of the land] is based on the nature, the fault is fundamentally in the principle; the land arises from the Buddha, yet the principle is fully present within ordinary beings and sages alike.

If one posits that [the object] is established as a substantial entity (*dravya*), what fault is incurred? If one posits that it is established as a nature (*svabhāva*), the attachment to that nature must be refuted;
yet even the refutation of that nature is spoken of in terms of "functioning" (*kriyā*). Thus, the three types of visible objects are refuted without needing further discussion.

To speak of "functioning" means that because there is ultimately no self or other, it causes the proponent to incur the fault of [falling into] causelessness. As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* (or *Cintāmaṇi-sūtra-śāstra*) regarding defilement and purity: [it reaches...]

If one travels through this land and examines it, asking whether the impure lands are so exceptionally distinct [from the pure lands], the answer is that since their causes are the same, their fruits should not differ.

For example, just as the retribution for wholesome causes in an impure land results in the fruits of human or celestial rebirth, why is it that in the various pure lands, although the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*) also exist, the resulting retribution is forever different from that of this land?

The intended meaning of the reply is that while they share the same activity (*samakārya*) and the same understanding (*samādhyavasāya*), they differ in their vows (*praṇidhāna*). This is like the case of "cessation-merit" (*śamathapuṇya*).
This is because, through the cultivation of vows and practices for the sake of stillness and goodness, the various lands differ in their hierarchical gradations;

while the names "human" and "deva" remain the same, their meanings differ according to the specific land. Regarding the mention of "two places," this is discussed here by contrasting the pure and the defiled.

As for the seven kinds of birth-and-death in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, as explained in the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation), they are like Indra’s net, wherein a single land encompasses all.
Because it encompasses all lands, this realm universally includes the two lower realms; however, it alone cannot include the superior realm of *Sukhāvatī* (Peaceful Light).

Since this principle is universally applicable, how could its logic be obstructed or differentiated? Based on this, one should explain that while the superior can include the inferior, there are further cases where it also includes the internal and external afflictions (*kleśa*) within the *sahā-loka* (the world of endurance), as their characteristics differ. Thus, those who have severed the afflictions of the internal realm and those who have not severed them [are both included].

Regarding the retributions of those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings before they reach the stages of abiding: although their paths of contemplation are common, they have not yet seen the principle.

Therefore, when discussing the relative superiority or inferiority of their retributive characteristics, they remain separated by the fact that the causes cultivated are not fixed. This lack of fixity arises because, during the time of cultivating the cause, pure and impure objects are fused, such that they cannot be designated as either identical or different;
hence it is said they are "not fixed. In the first stage (*bhūmi*) and beyond of the Separate Teaching, there are the seven purities.

This is the interpretation of our own school (Jinkashi). Regarding the establishment of the seven names, "the first five have their substance fulfilled" (*taiman*): since "substance" (*tai*) occupies the initial position, the first four all achieve the substance;
however, these only accomplish the primary retribution (*shōhō*). Therefore, the fifth is required for the place of residence, which is the secondary retribution (*eihō*).
Because both the primary and secondary retributions are complete, it is called "fulfillment of substance. Furthermore, because the preceding four adorn the substance, [it is placed] at the beginning.

The essence possesses both characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*). The three and five [categories] belong to the characteristics: the three are the characteristics of the primary retribution (*samyag-vipāka-lakṣaṇa*), and the five are the characteristics of the secondary retribution (*upapatti-bhājana-lakṣaṇa*).

The two and four belong to the functions: the two are for the benefit of others, and the four are for one's own benefit. If this is so, why are the characteristics and functions presented in an alternating manner rather than sequentially? Answer:

Although the primary and secondary [retributions] pertain to both self and others, they are paired separately for the sake of convenience. Although the sixth and seventh [categories] are called "causes" (*hetu*), [they are not].

Since it is admitted that the "fulfillment of the perfect fruit" (*phala-paripūri*) is present in the first stage (*bhūmi*), this refers to establishing cause and effect by viewing the first stage in relation to the stages prior to it;
thus, the perfection of this cause is termed the fulfillment of the fruit. As for "the eternally quiescent light" (*nitya-prabhāsvara*), this is fundamentally the true object (*viṣaya*).

This intends to clarify that the essence of the object and wisdom (*jñāna*) is inherently fused; therefore, it is said to be "identical with the eternally quiescent nature of wisdom. Wisdom is that which illumines.

To explain what is intended to clarify that while the sequence is the same, the departure [from delusion] differs because the essence is distinct—since the object and the wisdom differ—it is said that they are "partially true.

Quoting the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* further proves that the wisdom is the same. Following this, the present sutra provides proof for why they are the same by pointing to the nature of ignorance as the essence of wisdom.
This wisdom is the object; only when its essence is the same is it identical. For the nature of ignorance is also...

Because it is the nature of the objective realm (*viṣaya*), it is inconceivable. The term "objective realm" is established here as a conclusion because all that was previously explained is common to both wisdom and the objective realm.

Now, concluding with the objective realm, it is again established from the perspective of the realm itself; it is also called "the lower. Below this, the different names are listed above, while below, the body and land are clarified.
Reflect deeply on this meaning. All instances of the meaning of the "land" (*kṣetra*) explained in subsequent passages and in the various scriptural teachings are based upon this.

If one applies this intent and extends it further, the principle will be fully exhausted. Regarding "the collection of wisdom" (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*) and so forth: because the four wisdoms are in harmony, it is called "collection" (*saṃbhāra*);
because consciousness is transformed into wisdom, it is called "penetration" (*abhijñā*). The name "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) still applies to delusion;

therefore, only after wisdom is perfected does the name "penetration" become manifest. Taking it in this way, it is then called "Quiescent Light" (*śāntaprabhā*). Thus, this Pure Land consists solely of the Dharma.

Abiding in the Dharma-body, it is not by way of form that it is named "Supreme"; rather, it is through the body adorned with various practices and vows that one truly evokes the Dharma-nature and the tranquil light of the land.
Only when both body and land are thus adorned can they be called "the adornment of the non-adorned. This is what is meant by saying that the fulfillment of the body and land is perfectly analogous.

Although the scriptures list different names for the lands—such as including those associated with the beings to be transformed—their explanations remain consistent despite these differences in terminology.
The interlocutor asks again: "Regarding this scripture and others, the interpretation of their meaning contradicts the sūtras; where does the logic for this lie? The answer is as follows:

The intention should be understood according to the Esoteric Teaching (Guhyamantra), wherein a single sound is interpreted differently. Thus, it encompasses both the Exoteric and Esoteric, being indeterminate in both senses.

As for the horizontal interpretation, it is as previously cited from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: because one perceives the two higher realms within this very land, the Lesser Vehicle is disparaged.

"Purifying and being unstartled" refers to the incident where [the Buddha] pressed the earth with his toe; even if one speaks of the "Great Vertical" (the vertical path), for those of lesser understanding it remains a horizontal standard according to correct principle.
It is not that [this teaching] is not heard as superior; [one should] examine the ten kinds of pure lands in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Someone says that the sūtra clarifies twenty-seven kinds of pure lands—one should examine this. One knows directly that this sūtra is not merely the cause for reaching [those lands].
From the mind up to the ten wholesome deeds are called both the "direct cause" (*samyag-hetu*) and the "supporting cause" (*āśraya-hetu*).

Regarding these two types of supporting causes—namely, one's own practice and benefiting others—it is precisely this [latter] that constitutes benefiting others by taking up soil. Only when self and other mutually establish the meaning of "soil" is its full significance realized;

they are merely explained differently according to the occasion and the capacity of the recipient. Thus, the supporting cause for benefiting beings arises from the addition of specific vows; therefore, the bodhisattva’s practice is based on a single cause.

The two aspects of upward-seeking constitute one's own practice as the basis, while transforming others constitutes the objective realm; within this transformation of others, the two are further divided into the distinct categories of self-practice and the reliance upon the objective realm for benefiting others.

Thus, one knows that the reliance and the object of one’s own practice are established through a single cause, which is why it is called the "True Cause" (zhengyin) that evokes the four Buddha-fruit realms.

Furthermore, because the reliance upon the fruit is likewise evoked by this cause, it is said to evoke the four lands of reliance. Therefore, although the cause is not different, [the fruits and their corresponding lands differ].
Because the meanings are divided into two distinct categories, the *Sāmbhogakāya* (Peaceful Light) and the *Dharmakāya* appear different, yet they are eternally one; this is a minor obstacle.
If one considers the relationship between the four teachings and the four lands, although there is this principle, it is not without slight differences. Why?

Because when the *Zàng* and *Tōng* [teachings] are compared with the Land of Shared Dwelling, and the [distinct] [teachings] are compared with the Land of Residual Existence, it seems as though they are somewhat attained. However, if one distinguishes the number of teachings within each land, then—
Because it would be inconvenient, I shall further discuss the provisional and ultimate teachings in detail regarding their increase and decrease.

When beings of the Separate and Perfect [teachings] come to be born in that land, they are still referred to as "Separate" and "Perfect" during the period when those provisional teachings remain in use. However, once they reach the stage of the True Reward Land (*sahōkappan*), they lose the designation of the Separate Teaching and become solely the eternally abiding Perfect [Teaching].
Thus, using the name of this land, I shall quote the *Lotus Sūtra* on longevity to show that this state continues until the end of the future.
The "measure" (pramāṇa) refers to citing the ultimate fruit to certify the provisional fruit. Thus, if the past is eternal, the future must necessarily be eternal.
Just as one descends from the fundamental fruit to manifest traces, one displays the practice of the Pure Land to attract sentient beings.

When discussing the Buddhas who are visible, one still relies on the three lands; yet, when discussing the *sāntaprabhā* (constant light) and the *nirnimitta* (signless) *śāntaprabhā*, all three are extinguished.
Because that which is invisible can become visible, a question is asked: "The Sūtra says 'going'—this is a general inquiry. First, the Sūtra is cited to establish the thesis;

the section beginning with "Is this... constitutes the objection. The intent of the objection is as follows: Is it that originally there was only one kind of rice color, yet it appears different by itself?
Or is it that originally there were many colors, yet they appear different? According to the answer provided below, since there are four propositions, how could this be [the case]?
It consists of merely one or two additional lines. Within this, the question and answer involve a total of three layers of fourfold analysis (*catuskoṭi*).
Since it is stated that "seeing is possible within the invisible," this refers to the *sambhogakāya* (Peaceful Light) in relation to the three lands.

First, the *sāvaśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana with remainder) subsumes the two co-resident lands (*sahabhūmi*). Based on these two co-resident lands, the fourfold analysis is established; for both lands possess substantial reality.

By distinguishing between similarities and differences, one may first establish the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) by comparing the *dharmatā-nirmāṇa* (essential transformation) with the two lower lands to determine existence and non-existence.

Second, within the *vipāka-nirmāṇa* (retribution transformation), one distinguishes its difference from the two lower lands by noting that while its form is unobstructed, the latter possess physical obstruction.

Third, by comparing the *śāntaprabhāsvara* (tranquil light) land with the three lower lands, one establishes another set of four propositions; herein, the form and substance of the tranquil light land are eternally quiescent.

Therefore, the four [categories] are distinguished by means of the relative opposition of existence and non-existence. Thus, the previous discussion of the second tetralemma was based on whether there is a material substance (*rūpa-dravya*) and whether it is obstructed or unobstructed.
Within the first tetralemma, we further distinguish the four specific cases based on obstruction.

If that is so, one should likewise establish another tetralemma prior to the first one, concerning pure substance and defiled vision—such as in the case of Śāriputra and others, where there is pure substance and pure vision.

Seeing [the land] as pure, like those in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), is seeing one's own impure body as pure; seeing it as impure, like those in the five turbidities, is seeing one's own impure body as impure.

These two are compared and contrasted as being in the same dwelling. Now, regarding the first four phrases, it says that "distinctive and perfect bodhisattvas use the divine eye" to see the land, for they should not use any other eyes;
this refers to the eyes of these two types of people at the stage of worthiness (*śaikṣa*). This...
Speaking in terms of the physical body residing in this land, if we discuss the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), those who see the two realms cohabiting must necessarily share the same substance.

Next, within the context of a single substance being seen by a single person, it clarifies that five types of people together perceive the "remaining" [reality], with no further distinctions among them.

Although these five types include both the Separate (*pratyekabuddha*) and Perfect (*bodhisattva*) vehicles, this is stated according to the common perception shared by the two vehicles of the Tripiṭaka and the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching.
Since those of the two teachings and three vehicles here all receive the provisional teaching, their vision regarding the realm of "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa) is not yet far-reaching;
thus, they merely share the same view of the land of "two together dwelling" (sāmbhogika-kāya) as being identical to that realm of "with remainder.

However, if within that land one gives rise to the mind of the Distinct or Complete [teachings], one immediately becomes identical to the vision of the Distinct or Complete. [Question: Why is it based on the realm of "with remainder" and so forth?

If it is said that "one substance and one vision" both have a remainder, then even if two [beings] dwell together and each sees for themselves, this could still be called "one substance and one vision.
Why must it necessarily be defined in terms of having a remainder? In the subsequent answer, it says:

"As for the three persons, one should know that the 'three kinds of mind-made beings' mentioned in the fourth phrase of the previous explanation refers to those of sharp and dull faculties among the *pratyekabuddhas* (those who attain realization through conditions)."

The text does not specifically point to the sharp faculties within the [śrāvaka] perspective; this is because this bodhisattva merely severs the common delusions, which is the same as the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), as he has just emerged from the common path.
Therefore, in the response, it first points to the three vehicles being identical in their vision of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Since these [vehicles] were originally distinct but are now all made identical, they are spoken of as such for the time being. If one were to point to the identity between the two [types of practitioners], [it would be as follows].

Those dwelling within this land perceive it according to their own station; there is nowhere they do not reach, yet for the sake of distinguishing between them, such explicit clarification is required.

As for the statement that the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) are "identical in one respect," this refers to the fact that when one has not yet given rise to the distinct or perfect mind, and has not yet seen into the Middle Way, the situation is equal;
thus, in the context of the Truth of Reality (*tattva-satya*), they are seen as identical. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also speaks of "rebirth" (*upapatti*). Furthermore—
Regarding the phrase "named 'coming to birth' because they look toward one another": (upon examination), the same applies to the next two lands.

Since it is thus that the two *sahā* (concordant) lands look toward each other, it is likewise for the remaining two lands when looking toward one another. To say "it is thus" merely refers to the distinction between horizontal and vertical:
while the two *sahā* lands look horizontally toward each other, the names of the other two lands are termed "vertical. If this is so, one may only go from the *Sahā* world to [the others].
Question: Why does the Pure [Land] produce these beings from within its own purity? Answer: The eight lower grades cannot be reborn in the highest grade;
rather, they are able to reach that land immediately because they have already attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"These people abandon their own pure karmic retribution and come to delight in this place of much anger and harm. This refers only to the Constantly Quiescent Light (*sadā-praśānta-prabhāsvara*), as there is no such text regarding the other levels.

Regarding the meaning of "going," it may be so for the superior grade; however, the meaning applies to both the middle and lower grades. This is because if there were no real recompense in the middle and lower grades, they would not exist at all;
furthermore, since the middle and lower grades of the *Sakyām-prabhāsa* (Peaceful Light) realm still pertain to the real recompense, the principle holds.

Moreover, if one establishes the meaning as "not going" yet "going upward," this also applies to the superior grade. Thus, the term "Well-Gone One" (*Sugata*) is indeed significant. [This applies to] the Tathāgata.
The meaning of this is certainly not without its expedient means. As for "going," the meaning can be understood;

as for what is called "coming," it simply refers to the aspiration to come, which should apply to Bodhisattvas. The principle is the same for those who have received their prediction from a minor stage.

Furthermore, regarding the mention of "humans and devas" within the Pure Land, that land possesses all the devas of the desire and form realms, though it lacks the Mount Sumeru where those dwelling on earth reside. (1)

All [stages] abide in dependence upon empty space, as detailed in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) regarding the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra-yāna*) and the final mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).
According to principle, the Separate Teaching should speak of "abiding" and "tending toward" (*mukha-pratipanna*);

that it does not do so here is because, although those who have already attained abiding are identical to the five types of persons of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings in their cultivation of the Middle Way and their subsequent birth in the land of remaining traces (*sa-upadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*), this is not the primary intent, and thus they are not included.

Regarding the essential substance, it is simply stated that one establishes "perfect faith" (*pariniṣpanna-śraddhā*) at the ten stages of practice (*daśa-pratipatti*). Furthermore, as for the mention of the "final mind" (*paścima-citta*), those from the seventh stage of faith (*saptama-śraddhā*) upward may also attain rebirth;
this is merely an abbreviated statement. First, concerning the passage from "the samādhi of correct reception" (*samādhi-samyak-pratisamvit*) up to "subduing ignorance" (*avidyā-vinodana*):

the explanation of the three types of "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*) all uses the term "fearing" (*śaṅkate*). This is out of reverence for the sacred scriptures and simultaneously demonstrates the absence of attachment. These three levels of progression are established according to the sūtras.

Regarding the meaning of the text, what kind of teaching or samādhi-samāpatti does this contain? If one refers to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), it applies from the seventh stage upward, or even up to the ninth stage;
as for the term "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva), it refers to dwelling separately while being identical to the Shared [Teaching], and thus one should take the ten practices (daśa-caryā).

Since the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) speaks of subduing ignorance, this refers to the stage of the seven levels of faith (saptaviṃśati-śraddhā) onward. Therefore, when the Separate Teaching (Biejiao) speaks of "intrinsic nature," if one does not perceive the Middle Way, then...

Not seeing the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena, those who have not yet initiated true cultivation [should understand] the meaning of "true conditions" (*bhūtapratyaya*). Regarding the meaning of these conditions, there are both general and specific senses. If categorized according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), there are two meanings:

first, that which is called "intention" (*manas*) because it has not yet reached the ultimate; second, that which is called "intention" because it involves the words of the Path of Teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) and the process of subduing. If the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyavyavasthāna*) are judged, they comprise three types. [The text continues: ...the three together are named "intention"; the three together enter the stages (*bhūmi*). One is merely that which has not yet reached the ultimate, thus named "intention. Two involves the words of the Path of Teaching and the terminology of subduing, thus named "intention. If the Ten Stages of the Shared Teaching are judged, they comprise three types.

Regarding the phrase "the mind and so forth," one should understand by analogy that what was previously clarified—namely, "one substance and one seeing"—refers to the two vehicles and the three types of *manomayakāya* (mind-born bodies) within the current teaching.
That "one substance and one seeing" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*) should be understood as resolving the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*;

thus, one should know that for those of the Distinct and Complete Teachings (*bheda-vyavahāra* and *pariniṣpanna*), there are three types of intention. Therefore, [the text] now separately proceeds from...

This is explained by applying it generally to the Bodhisattvas. A question is raised: from the stage of *fen-duan* (segmented birth) up to the *guobao-tu* (land of retribution), since the afflictions of *jian-xi* (view-delusion) and *si-xi* (thought-delusion) are common to all, their severance should be identical, and thus their relinquishing of the body and subsequent responses [to rebirth] should be equal.

Furthermore, regarding the taking of birth in the *shibbao-tu* (land of true retribution) and so forth, if one refers back to the previous discussion of the three lands having birth while only the *chang-ji-guang* (eternally quiescent light) land is free from coming and going, then [the former cases of birth] would logically not be consistent [with the latter].

Furthermore, regarding the intent behind this question and answer: it merely seeks to re-emphasize that meaning is understood by following the names; moreover, it refers to those of middling and inferior capacities who remain within the realm of karmic retribution (*vipāka*).

It is in terms of retribution that "arising" is discussed, and thus there is a discussion of limits regarding karmic retribution. However, as for the limit of what is entered into, that is not karmic retribution;

rather, the very limit of what is entered into is the realization of the Truth (*tattva-darśana*). Therefore, it is said that for those of the highest capacity, there is no retribution and thus no arising.

Only the True [Dharmadhātu] is non-arising; yet that which is called "arising" arises from non-arising. Therefore, within the fruit of retribution (vipāka), the True is also seen to possess the meaning of the fruit of retribution arising from non-arising.

To speak of the ultimate, the Land of Peaceful Light (Sukhāvatī) is solely the True, and in terms of the principle that it eternally lacks the fruit of retribution, one may also say it possesses the meaning of non-arising arising. This, however, is such that there is no further arising. Question: If...

Regarding the phrase "non-arising arising" and so forth, the intent of this question is as follows: since both "non-arising arising" and "non-constant constancy" are expressed through the force of linguistic parallelism, their meanings appear to be contradictory;
therefore, the question is posed using these contrary meanings. In the response, the intent is that although the names differ, the meaning is the same.
Why then is it said they "appear similar"? It is because this principle is accepted, and thus the words of agreement are granted. As for what follows below:

The explanation clarifies that while the names differ, the meaning is identical. To discuss this thoroughly: it is merely a matter of naming "permanence" as "permanence" and "non-arising" as "non-arising.
Thus, citing the state of the Sage is precisely the permanence within impermanence and the arising within non-arising.
Although the truth of the forty-one stages is non-arising and does not arise, because other traces of ignorance remain, it is termed "the view of impermanence with a portion of permanence."

Therefore, it is named "Constantly Contemplating the Visible. Regarding the subsequent question on the "Visible," the answer states: "That which is spoken of as the Original Vow refers to the Superior Grade Pure Land;

there is no need to open the gradual teaching, hence it is said that 'by virtue of the vow, there can be speaking. Because the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) land lacks such a vow, it cannot be spoken of;
since it is not spoken of, it is not heard, and thus [the interlocutor] comes to inquire. It is like the trees in the realm of Sukhāvatī preaching suffering, emptiness, and [non-self]."
Regarding the statement that "the opening [of the provisional] for arhats does not say 'may it be verified that the stage is not high,'" the *Lotus Sūtra* and other texts contain two meanings here:

first, they universally certify the opening of all provisional teachings; second, they specifically certify the gradual approach of the two vehicles, both of which are the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and therefore these texts are cited.

If one follows the perspective of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), this refers only to the opening of the teaching (*jiaokai*) and not the opening of the principle (*likai*), though it may also involve the opening of the principle.

To demonstrate this within the Perfect [Truth]: if one considers the retribution of karmic fruit up to the Dharma taught, from the perspective of retribution, one must speak of Suffering and its Accumulation;

because suffering and accumulation exist, the Four Truths must be complete. Within the retribution of karmic fruit, when distinguishing the Land of Tranquil Light (Sukhāvatī), it must be explained from the standpoint of Principle;

therefore, it possesses only the meaning of the Truth of Cessation. Furthermore, regarding the teaching of the Dharma in the Land of Tranquil Light, the two lands should be distinguished in a similar manner.
There are others who maintain that the "Shared" [Land] and the "Common" [Land] are both horizontally equivalent to the Land of Quiescent Light (Jigōdo).

If within the Shared Land it is also said to be "immeasurable," this is because it is contrasted with the One Reality (Ijjitsu); or it is said to be "universal" because it is contrasted with the One Reality.

Therefore, if the One Reality is spoken of within the Shared Land, then by analogy, the teaching of the Land of Dharma-Reality and the Land of Recompense (Hōpō) within the Shared Land should also be understood as such. However, these are discussed in terms of horizontal equivalence.

Regarding the four abodes, the remaining three gradually decrease; this can be seen by applying the same principle. If one includes the identity of essence, all are fourfold. As for contemplating the mind as the four lands:

first, the nature of the mind is established as the principle *sambhogakāya* (principle *sambhogakāya*, or *dharmadhātu-sambhogakāya*); subsequently, it is explained that sentient beings, being deluded regarding this *sambhogakāya*, perceive the three lands.
Alternatively, they may lose the One Truth and perceive the Four Truths. Within this, first there is a general clarification of the causes for their arising, followed by [the specific details].
Below "Ignorance" (avidyā), the objects of delusion are specifically shown; next, below "The Middle Way," the contemplation of the mind is correctly explained to establish the four lands.

Regarding the profound purport of the text of this chapter: the meaning of the text in this chapter encompasses both the introduction and the main body; within the introduction, the manifestation of entering the correct [path] is perfectly clear.
Below, in the main exposition, the profound purport lies here: "Within this realm, the karma of fetters has not yet been severed," and so forth. (Upper Capital)

(“Guǎn” [in the first instance] is pronounced as above; “dú guǎn” [in the second instance] is pronounced as below. However, it is not that they have completely severed birth, nor is it that they have not at all severed the two kinds of beings who come to be born here.

This statement is made because those in the "Skillful Means" chapter rely on two teachings, and furthermore, through these two teachings alone, they exhaustively sever the coming of births to that land. This is explained in the "Disciples" chapter.

Because the three vehicles are rebuked, there are likewise only those of the three vehicles who come to be born there; thus, while those of the three vehicles come to be born and reach that place, they receive only two teachings.

The titles may be compared with the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) to see the correspondences; now, by pointing out one or two sections here and providing a comparative analysis, they will be easy to understand.

"Now, at the beginning of this text" refers to the Worldly Truth (*loka-saṃvṛti*). Furthermore, "likewise" [refers to] "benefiting the good and faithful" as the Truth for Others (*para-artha*), and "moreover, the *Dazhilun*" [refers to] the Truth of Counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).

As for the points raised in the *Fahua shuji* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) regarding the inquiry into the Vinaya concerning the proper time for eating and so forth:

these were provisional regulations established for the sake of distinguishing [the Buddhist community] from outsiders; one should not seek ultimate truth within them. The intent of the teaching lies solely in seeking liberation and the wondrous principle of true suchness (*tathatā*).
When citing the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Avataṃsaka* sutras within the context of "provisional names based on causes and conditions," it is merely following the perspective of kalpas.

Realizing that [dharmas] are merely provisional designations does not mean that both Sūtra and Sautrāntika schools maintain that all things exist as mere designations; rather, because that school frequently asserts such a view, we borrow their terminology here.

Regarding the analogy of using gold coins to buy copper coins: when a sage speaks of "self" and "person," there is nothing strange about it, just as Ānanda partook of food [without violating the precepts].

the present mention of the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* is merely based on various passages within its conventional manifestation (*vyavahāra*), and does not mean it is explained in the Hīnayāna.
Ānanda was able to uphold both the Great and Small [vehicles], as there are many such varieties; it is not possible for one person to uphold only a single Hīnayāna Piṭaka.

Regarding the question "How can there be... and so forth, the intent of this inquiry is as follows: if one speaks of a "self" in accordance with worldly convention, then all four teachings should equally involve such a self;
since the self is conventional, how can one further establish the names "sovereign" (*īśvara*) and "non-dual"? The intent of the response is as follows:

while the three [lower] teachings follow worldly sentiment and for the most part belong to the conventional, even though they are distinct, when compared to the Perfect Teaching, they remain conventional. Furthermore, within the Separate Teaching, those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) have not yet contemplated non-duality.
Although the final mind realizes [this], according to the teaching it cannot be called "eternal mastery. In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it is clarified that "I" is precisely the hearer;
because both the capacity to hear and that which is heard are the Dharma-realm, it causes me to realize that there is no hearing external to this.

The statement in the Great Sūtra that "birth-and-birth" (*sheng-sheng*) refers to the uninterrupted continuity of the twelve links of dependent origination is because the phenomenon of birth-and-birth is conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Thus, it is comprehensive.

Regarding the teaching of "not hearing what is heard" and the distinct teaching of "hearing what is not heard," if one consults various texts, why is it that these two phrases are applied interchangeably between the teaching and the present text?
This is because their meanings are mutually pervasive, allowing them to be used interchangeably; however, this is not the case for the original text of the sutra itself.
Since both are expounded according to specific meanings, they may be discussed interchangeably, as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* explains "hearing" by means of "arising" and so forth.
The sequence of the arising phrase and the hearing is also equal; this extends even to the explanation of arising, which is likewise so. Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:

"Arising and non-arising, non-arising and arising, arising and non-arising, non-arising and non-arising. Thus, from the perspective of meaning, they are mutually interchangeable and have no fixed location.

As for how the meaning is universally applicable, why does the teaching explain "hearing what was not heard"? Although [the ear] is obstructed, as for the color-form, it is "hearing what was not heard."
To provide a separate explanation of the statement "form is itself emptiness": the "hearing" that arises from the "not-hearing" is like planting a tree in empty space;
though it is planted, it is empty. Both meanings apply here. What benefit is there in clinging to the names?

If one asks whether there are no such things as the marks of hearing and so forth, this is a question posed by citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* from the fourth phrase. I fear that those who do not understand might see [this as a contradiction].

Regarding the fourth phrase, "not hearing, not hearing," it further explains that the characteristics [of hearing] are exhausted, meaning that hearing is forever absent because it is contrary to the characteristic of hearing.
Therefore, one must pose a question to initiate the subsequent answer. This intention is to reveal that when the hearing of the two types of death is exhausted, the hearing of mastery arises;
thus, the answer states: "If it is exhausted in a similar manner, one can hear in a similar manner; if it is ultimately exhausted, one can hear ultimately. Thus ends the question.
Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, the previous question should have been phrased: "If all [beings] are designated as 'worldly renown' (*loka-pravāda*), what true self exists?
Now, the question should instead be: "How can it be that all are made to be non-existent? To further discuss existence here would contradict the question itself.

If this is so, the meaning of the concluding refutation in the response is as follows: if there were definitely an existence, there could not be the four [alternatives]; if there were definitely a non-existence, that too could not be.
Fourth, if one does not permit [the provisional teachings], there are two faults: first, the fault of destroying the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*) teaching;
for when skillful means is contrasted with reality, it consists of four types. Second, the fault of increasing the unbelief of those who lack faith and thereby destroying the true teaching;

for those who do not believe will not accept that the Buddha has various teachings to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings, and thus they will still reject the correct meaning of the various doctrinal systems of the Buddha-dharma.

Even within the Tripiṭaka teachings—which are not believed by those who lack faith—there are still three passages that clarify the difference between my provisional and real [self], establishing and refuting one another to demonstrate that my [self] is not non-existent. Furthermore, the latter three teachings all clarify the existence of the self;
therefore, one should know that it cannot be non-existent. Nevertheless, while the existence of the self is admitted, it must not be taken as fixed or singular in its intent.

Both provisional and ultimate teachings coexist to respond to challenges; for in the Buddha-dharma there is no self, we know that each school establishes its own tenet according to its own inclination.

Within the provisional teachings of the Tripitaka, such doctrines are already numerous, let alone when the three provisional teachings are contrasted with the one ultimate reality—their names are not uniform.
How can one unilaterally claim that "there is no self"? Thus, we know that whether [the self] exists or does not exist is not non-Buddhist; this is the Great Treatise.

Regarding "the aggregates, bases, and so forth": "holding" (dhātu) means to maintain or sustain, each having its own distinct portion, like objects within a mountain that do not overlap with one another.
Since the aggregates, bases, and so forth are substantial entities, they do not include conventional designations such as time, number, or the sequence of the precepts.

As for the ancient *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, there is a prologue at the beginning of the sūtra. Regarding "a single moment of the patience toward suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*): since one has not yet emerged from meditative observation, there is no hearing of the Dharma.
The meaning relies on what was previously heard to enter the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*). This takes a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) as "one time.

Next, regarding the application up to the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-door), these are also established based on four meanings to define the lands upon which the three bodies rely.

Therefore, the first three [bodies] are categorized according to the three virtues of nature (*prakṛti*), while the last one is categorized according to what is attained through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The three virtues arise from the blossoms of the seven factors of enlightenment; when the causal characteristics of compassion are established, one relies upon them to make vows.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies the parable of those who feel the elephant: if you maintain a literal interpretation that excludes the Dharma-gate, it is like each person grasping a different part of the elephant and thus mutually losing its true reality.

Therefore, in our school’s interpretation of the meaning, the two aspects of phenomena and principle are both perfect; is this not the attainment of the elephant in its entirety? It is just as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The answer is as explained in detail in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning). Regarding these four types of Saṃgha:

the first two [the Saṃgha of the Dharma and the Saṃgha of the Path] cannot be distinguished from those who are "harmonious in non-action" (*asamāhita*), because they are still unable to differentiate between the two treasuries of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Although it may be possible for them to be harmonious in action, their treasury of precepts (*śīla*) is not clear;

However, because the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* bodhisattvas in the *Tripiṭaka* and *Common* teachings are the same as those of the Small Vehicle, they were specifically excluded there.

As for their receiving the name in the Common teaching, each follows its own respective doctrine. My current use of the meaning of the preceding question and answer is intended to reclaim [the title].

This language of exclusion and praise is seen as pertaining to the non-essential aspects of the teaching, whereas the general praise constitutes the fivefold [classification] of the true essence of the doctrine.

Fifth, "but as for the assembly... and so forth provides an explanation according to the teachings (*yàojiào*). Within this explanation according to the teachings, there are two parts: first, the purpose of the introduction; second, the main body.

Regarding the explanation within this section, if one further distinguishes [the stages] according to their positions: when reaching this stage, one can then generally serve as a teacher and guide for sentient beings.

As for the formal praise, it is as found in the concluding text below; this refers to the position of the "Successor" (Upapadya-bhūmi). From here downward is the formal conclusion regarding the functions within the praised stage.
As for the mention of "co-residing" (*tongju*) and so forth, there are both the "fundamental" (*ben*) and the "traces" (*ji*). The fundamental refers to each teaching.

These are manifested as the cognitive subjects (*vijñāna*) of the three lands (*bhūmi*). As for their traces (*liṅga*), they are each subdivided according to the teachings and stages, corresponding to their respective lands;
this can be understood through reflection. Regarding the four characters "Great Wisdom" (*mahājñāna*) and "Fundamental Practice" (*mūlapratipatti*), there are two explanations:

in other contexts, the meanings are applied differently—the first appears to be a *karmadhāraya* (descriptive compound), while the second appears to be a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound). Because the ten wholesome actions are the foundation of all virtues, they pervade both the shallow and the deep; alternatively, they may represent the vessel world (*bhājana-loka*). However...
Since it has already been stated in the preceding text that "relying on the land" refers to the container world (*bhājanaloka*),
we know that here it merely indicates reliance on the small worlds within [the great trichiliocosm], such as the examples of a single mountain or a single continent.
In the sixth fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra*, it is said that those whose spiritual wisdom is sublime occupy the highest rank; because they are high, they are called "sublime.

If one follows the scriptural text, [the Bodhisattvas] who were together with the five hundred were not merely their peers, so how could they have been fit to follow them? If they were not among those being led, their rank must certainly be...
Descending to the passage where he requests [the Buddha] to speak, it still says that these five hundred and others have all already resolved their minds;

Since the fundamental locus is not included within the designation of "purity," it is now praised through the universal resonance of loftiness and brilliance.
Were it not for this loftiness, how could one know the manifestations and the auspicious omens revealed to correspond with the signs of the pure body and the pure land?
