Since the text does not state that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and the single dharma together encompass all dharmas, it is said for now that [this principle] applies universally.
Alternatively, one might say it pertains only to the Tripiṭaka Teaching; however, because the Tripiṭaka Teaching does not speak of "purity," it is simply not discussed here.

Although those who are exhorted to aspire toward the fruit by practicing the cause do so in relation to various dharmas, they do not yet equal those who fully comprehend the conditions; this is merely a matter of nomenclature.

The most prominent [teaching] regarding the attainment of the fruit still maintains the distinction between the Separate (Beda) and Perfect (Yuan) teachings; this is because "Manifest" (Xian) is established as a distinct name to show that it differs from the Zang and Tong [teachings].

Regarding the previous two teachings, when it is said that precepts, concentration, and wisdom arise from the fivefold dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*), within the provisional (expedient) teachings, the name "fivefold dharma-body" applies only to those who abide in the fruit.
Furthermore, although the three—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—pertain to both cause and fruit, [in this context they refer to the fruit].

Regarding the two kinds of liberation (*vimokṣa*), the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* maintain that they apply only to the stage prior to the fruit; the first four [liberations] receive their names only after one has attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
However, since we follow the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) here, the fifth applies to all four teachings. Because the fourfold perfection is listed, the meaning is not restricted to a single level;
thus the conclusion states: "one cultivates the five bodies. It further says: "Using these five bodies, one again gives rise to the Dharma-body; these five bodies are the five causes."
Because it pertains to the body, the initial general statement "fearing that" likely refers to a commonality rather than a specific one; it is a commonality.

In the first two of the five divisions of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), it says "as before," because offenses and non-offenses and so forth all take the five divisions of the preceding teaching as their object.

Thus, each subsequent teaching contemplates each preceding one. If there is a single sound with diverse understandings, then within a single set of five divisions, what is seen by each [individual] differs.

In the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Shared (Śrāvaka) Teachings, it is said that those who "see the True" have reached the ultimate perfection; however, this is not the "perfection" of the Perfect Teaching (Vajrayāna), for it is merely called "perfect" by virtue of reaching an ultimate limit.
Regarding the "ninefold precepts" and so forth: in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, each of the six perfections is divided into nine aspects, such that while the names are identical, their meanings differ.

Therefore, I now employ the textual structure of those three sets of nine to establish the three divisions, through which one clearly knows for oneself that the Dharma-body is manifested and so forth.

The former refers only to the realization of principle (*li*), while the latter encompasses both cause and effect across all stages of delusion and awakening, with each stage possessing its own manifestations and concealments.

When the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) states that, "at first glance, it is no different from the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*)," the intent is that both reach the same ultimate fruit of eternal abiding.

Nevertheless, there is a great difference in the objects and wisdom cultivated, as well as the causes and effects, between the two. Furthermore, when the Separate Teaching speaks of "nine kinds" in all three [stages], this generally refers to those prior to the stages (*diqian*).

Up to the realization of the path of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), they are identical; thus it is said there is "no distinction. Should one wish to proceed, further differentiation may be made.
Regarding the phrase "the three preceding teachings lack the principle of cultivating the five causes simultaneously," the term "equality" uses phenomena to illustrate principle;
thus it says "phenomenal equality. This refers to the Greatness of the Dharmakāya within the smallness of afflictions—great and small are eternally so, with no mutual opposition.
Furthermore, at the time of attaining the fruit, the great is always contained within the small; thus, the capacity for function allows a mustard seed to contain Mount Sumeru.
The term "uninterrupted" refers exclusively to the inconceivable Dharmakāya, which is fully present within a single thought-moment of an ordinary, base being.

This primordial state of mutual presence does not concern the penetration of physical objects; therefore, those who rely on the provisional gates of teaching are deluded regarding this inconceivable state of mutual presence.
Even if one hears the principle of permanence, because of the divergence between delusion and awakening, those of provisional capacity follow the teachings without yet reaching reality;

however, upon attaining the Grounds (*bhūmi*), their superior functions are no different [from those of the ultimate], and thus within the path of teaching they still remain subject to divergent interpretations.

Only in the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) is there suchness from beginning to end, so that the five bodies do not deviate from the ordinary physical substance. When wisdom and practice take the principle as their object, this is called the "Wisdom Body" (*prajñā-kāya*), which is cultivated through practice.
Because the characteristics of the causal stage serve as aids to concentration (*samādhi*), it is said for the time being that within these matters, wisdom (*prajñā*) is fully present;

yet, because these are various aspects of wisdom, one takes perfect wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-prajñā*) as the primary path. By using the primary to dissolve the auxiliary, there is nowhere they are not integrated, for the primary and auxiliary are practiced in union.
As for "the beginning mind" and so forth, all its intended meanings are as explained above; this passage is also [to be understood] in that way.

Because these are explained by way of analogy, one should know that "entering emptiness" takes the compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*) as its object of contemplation; therefore, in each of the preceding teachings, it is said that they take phenomena as their object (*dharmālambana*).

Thus, in the *Tripiṭaka* and *Shared* (Śrāvaka) vehicles, one reaches only up to the object of phenomena; in the *Distinct* (Pratyekabuddha) vehicle, one attains the objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) only at the final stage of the mind;

whereas in the *Perfect* (Bodhisattva) vehicle, one cultivates the three types of compassion from the very first moment of the mind. These four teachings comprise the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
As for "as previously explained," it is as explained earlier regarding the Buddha-lands; this is used as an exhortation for the practice of seeking [enlightenment].

Therefore, it is necessary to demonstrate or open up the six [pāramitās] into seventy, one hundred, and so forth. Regarding the seventy, they are fully detailed in the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation).
As for opening them into one hundred, each of the eleven [categories] further assists one another. As for the eighty thousand [dharmas] and so forth, these correspond to [the faculties of beings].

Regarding the statement that the samādhis, afflictions, dhāraṇīs, and so forth all number eighty thousand, they are so named because all those eighty thousand have reached the other shore (*pāramitā*).
As for the various *pāramitās*, it is because a single practice and a single mind all reach the other shore.

"Expedient means" (*upāya*) is as previously stated, such as in the explanation of the title of the "Chapter on Expedient Means. It refers to the expedient means for generating the fruit-ground *dharmakāya*.

This is because they lead through to the perfect fruit. Since the causes encompass both one’s own practice and the full benefit of others, the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are themselves the fruit;

yet they are also said to "arise from the six supernormal powers" because when practice is not yet perfected, although one speaks of the five powers, this merely defers to the fruit—though in reality, one has already attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) powers.
Thus, the six fruits arise from the six causes. This distinction between the separate and the perfect is also a metaphorical borrowing.
Since this is the name of the fruit, we know that there are also six divisions within the cause that result in the six fruits. As for the initial observation regarding "the distant" and so forth:

because karma is the fundamental basis from which one comes, while in the Separate and Perfect [Teachings] it is delusion regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*) that serves as the fundamental basis, it is said that even beyond the realms (*dhātu*), one should further speak of the nine periods of time. Third, it is also possible to derive [the distinctions] from the cause.

The name takes the inconceivable wisdom of time as its essence. Regarding the passage in the latter part of this sutra and so forth, if one follows this intent, it pertains solely to the Perfect [Teaching] and does not even extend to the Distinct [Teaching];
yet, by using this as a point of reference, one can also understand how it applies universally.

The contemplation of principle and phenomena (*li-shi*) constitutes the subjective capacity for cognition (*neng-yuan*), while principle and phenomena themselves constitute the objective objects of cognition (*suo-yuan*). This is explained in detail in the *Zhi-guan* (Calming and Contemplation), concerning the primary and auxiliary practices.

This refers to the fact that the various teachings differ in their approaches to *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight); since these two are distinct, the phenomena they manifest are likewise different. To speak of them collectively:

the ultimate reality is termed "principle" (*li*), while the provisional is all categorized as "phenomena" (*shi*). The realization of the Dharmakāya of the Buddha-fruit through *samādhi* and *prajñā* constitutes both the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* at the stage of fruition;
it is also the union of tranquility and illumination, the two virtues, the two wisdoms, and the two adornments.
Although non-dual, they are divided into two to distinguish the four teachings and their respective retributions; these three [categories] all rely on the "equal" [teaching].
As for the four teachings, the fruit of Buddhahood in all of them possesses the ten powers and so forth. These three [powers] exist only in the fruit;

since the previous [section] explained generally that the causal person possesses them, the present text uses the phrase "provisionally" (*yǒngwǎng*). Regarding "arising from the true," this refers to what is entered.
Regarding the names, all teachings on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) are none other than reality; such pure phenomena (dharma) point toward the fact that all dharmas are equally pure.
Although the preceding section addressed this generally, one should know that the principle of purity is not provisional.
Furthermore, it should be understood that each of these dharma-gates individually contains and subsumes the others, just as the first two adornments subsume the ten subsequent ones.

The second [category] consists of that which is clarified in the "Compendium of Methods for Stopping and Contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-saṃgraha-dharma*) and that which subsumes the Buddha’s majestic deportment through the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*);

this is its characteristic. In summary, these do not go beyond constantly contemplating *nirvāṇa* while practicing the Path, for *prajñā* and liberation constitute the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*).
Regarding the phrase "expounding with a single voice," this is a further conclusion made using "single voice" to ensure it accords with the intent of the Sūtra.
Therefore, while the former was called "extensive exhortation" (*guǎngquàn*) and this is called "concluding exhortation" (*jiéquàn*),

although it would have been consistent with the preceding chapter to call this too "extensive," the fact that it is not so here suggests that within the "extensive exhortation" itself, two further divisions were made. It is likely that only the first chapter was initially divided into two,
and there is no reason for a second division because one does not wish to cause unnecessary prolixity.
*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, Scroll 11:
Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* as taught by the Buddha, up to the point of "those who have not yet entered the stage," they abandon what they have previously received. (Examination:

Because [the term] "Mahāyāna" and so forth are spoken according to the common division [of the canon], it is said that they are "many. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Śrāvaka sūtras, the Bodhisattva is regarded as being like a son; [this is] not yet..."
Because they have severed delusions, the Śrāvakas are regarded as true sons; because they have severed delusions, the Mahāyāna sūtras regard Bodhisattvas as true sons.
Because they seek the ultimate fruit, the Śrāvakas are regarded as semblance sons; because they do not aspire to the Great [Vehicle], their intentions may coincide for the time being.

Regarding those of superior capacity, even in the three turnings of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Śāriputra is taken as the representative of the highest root; here too, he occupies the initial position in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
He immediately took Kāśyapa and the other four as those of medium capacity; just as this sutra follows after Śāriputra, the *Lotus Sutra* takes Ānanda as those of inferior capacity.
Because there are slight differences regarding the "medium" category—this sutra including the remainder of those with the nine virtues—it is said that they are "roughly similar.
However, as for the passage beginning "But the Tathāgata," it is like first establishing the state and expanding the borders to achieve merit, which relies upon loyal ministers.

Regarding those who serve as intimate advisors and assistants while secretly practicing the precepts: although Upāli was the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya, he lacked a reputation for secrecy;

thus, in matters of the secret [mind], he could not equal Rāhula. As for the "eight seats of ministers," namely the two *puye* (vice-presidents) and the six *shangshu* (ministers of state), they correspond to the ten mental factors (*caitasika*).
In this context, I have listed them according to the names used in the old translations; if translated according to the new terminology, these would be sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

Regarding the mental factors of volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), wisdom (*prajñā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), attention (*manasikāra*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), and concentration (*samādhi*), which are present in all states of mind:

if one looks at these according to their traditional names, they are simply designated as "contact" (*sparśa*) and "feeling" (*vedanā*). While the specific designations for these two differ, all other names are identical;
thus, these two names are merely different terms for the same meaning. The Buddha, as the King of Dharma, has [taught] these most excellent mental factors. Thus it was asked.

Question: Since both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) require both primary and auxiliary practices, why is it that one employs "primary practice" during the path of seeing and "auxiliary practice" during the path of cultivation?

Answer: There are two reasons for this. First, one distinguishes between primary and auxiliary by comparing phenomena with phenomena, and by observing principle (*li*) versus observing phenomena (*shi*).
Second, from the perspective of the person: once one has entered the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and attained the stage of the primary position, from that point onward [the distinction is made].
Furthermore, by cultivating the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*) as an auxiliary to manifest the correct principle, one achieves the latter three fruits;

moreover, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), this is because one practices through the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*). Next, regarding the phrase "until entering nirvāṇa," as for what is called the "ten dharma-gates" (*daśa-dharmamukha*), what is the intended meaning?
It does not merely refer to the worldly mental factors (*citta-caitasika*), but they also constitute dharma-gates. Why? Because if [they exist] in ordinary beings...

Now, as for the statement that "only by name is there existence" up to the four types of withered [trees], this means that within the state of being "withered by name," the aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth, constitute the Dharma-gate of withering.

Prosperity and the two negations (*ubhayābhāva*) are explained according to this same principle. Regarding the fact that these Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings are not fixed as either gradual or sudden, they do not go beyond sensation, perception, and the other aggregates.
Thus, the phrase "first appearing as if drawn in by a hook of desire" refers to these ten mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) which further interpenetrate one another.

Now, let us speak first from the perspective of the general desire within the worldly ten mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), and later explain how one is led to enter the Buddha’s ten numerical categories.
Within the section concerning Kāśyapa, the desire for all wholesome dharmas (*sarva-kuśala-dharma-kāma*) is taken as their basis.

Why is this specifically paired with Kāśyapa? The answer is that there are both general and specific meanings. While the general meaning may be so, if we discuss it according to its specific sense, we take only...
Therefore, Kāśyapa is now given his name among those with wholesome desires because he excels in the practice of *dhūta* (ascetic) virtues;

he is further distinguished as one who delights in doctrinal discussion (*vāda*). "Delight" (*sparśa*) here refers to contact (*sparśana*); it is so named because it involves an encounter and a reciprocal engagement with that [object].
This is explained according to ancient terminology, just as in the expressions "to touch upon speech" (*sparśa-vāk*) or "to touch upon hearing" (*sparśa-śravaṇa*). Its...
Regarding those who practice by means of mindfulness and counting, they are able to maintain the meaning;

furthermore, for those who uphold the Vinaya, it is most convenient to consider that "Secret Practice" (Mimixing) refers to one whose thoughts abide within such that no one can fathom them. This corresponds to Śūgiki (Śāriputra).

These two characters are divided into two applications: first, the explanation of the character's meaning corresponds to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); second, the two characters "liberation" (*vimukti*) clarify the function of emptiness. If...

One does not perceive emptiness without liberation through mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward an object; that which is called "recollection" (*smṛti*) is only designated as such when there is mental attention.

When the Buddha instructs one to engage in this counting and so forth, it is because when cultivating the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one takes the recollection of light and so forth as the skillful means;
thus, it is said that the mind is bound to an external object. The statement that "all ordinary beings possess this concentration" refers to the lifting of the mind.

Regarding the fixed number [of mental factors]: as in the fundamental dhyānas, all sentient beings have at some time attained them; therefore, it is said that "all possess" them. The passage beginning with "If there were none...

serves to prove the fixed number of mental factors (*caitta*). By citing those of inferior capacity who are unable to progress in the cultivation of the mind, it shows that if there were only the primary mind (*citta*) alone, it would merely be called "fixed" (*niyata*) and not "fixed in number" (*niyatasaṃkhyā*). As for the "four fascicles," the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* consists of four fascicles.
In ancient translations, the term for "feeling" (*vedanā*) was rendered as "suffering" (*tòng*), and the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* likewise refers to it as "feeling.
The reason for citing both names side by side is to clarify that "suffering" is indeed "feeling," lest people misunderstand.

Although the preceding section explained the "ten [categories]" based on the ten numerical groupings, here, regarding each of the ten individuals, we briefly speak of their "withering and flourishing," which corresponds to each person passing through these states.
Because the characteristics of the five flavors have not yet been manifested, it is said that "the words are few. Herein, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is primarily employed;
since *nirvāṇa* specifically symbolizes entering into the [Middle Way], it says, "placing all sons therein," and that he himself also enters therein.
Regarding the phrase "the ten disciples and others," the intention behind the Tathāgata’s entry is to cause all disciples to enter therein; this is the meaning.
From beginning to end, it also employs the text of the Great Sūtra’s Lion’s Roar and the words of the Lion’s Roar itself: "Who is able to adorn the twin śāla trees?
The Buddha’s response to this, as well as the words of the Lion’s Roar’s realization and understanding, are fully cited in the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation).

It states that the Tathāgata alone is most capable of adorning [the realm]; thus, one knows that only upon reaching the ultimate fruit does one receive the title of "most" (*parama*). One should understand this.
My disciples, you should understand that we have merely attained a small portion of the Tathāgata’s realization regarding that which is "neither withering nor flourishing.

If this were the case, it would not be only *nirvāṇa* that is termed "neither withering nor flourishing"; rather, all explanations of the Buddha-nature revealed throughout the Eight Teachings may be so named.

Whether in practice or in realization, they are all called *nirvāṇa* and all are called "adornments. One must contemplate this through the great purport of the *Lotus Sūtra* before one can truly see it.

Regarding the "two thousand," the intention is that they collectively comprise five hundred. Although the specific characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the Dharma-gates employed have not yet been manifested, because the Dharma-gates are pervasive and general, he asks again, saying:
"I have not yet seen these five hundred Dharma-gates; therefore, one may represent them by means of bodily causes.
Now, as for the count reaching five hundred, this merely borrows a number to correspond with a number; the essential point lies in the meaning.

Because these do not emerge from the faculties (*indriya*) or objects (*viṣaya*), they are employed to counteract them and eliminate the five hundred [afflictions]. Thus, the causes of the five hundred bodies are cited as evidence;

one thereby knows that the causes of the body do not emerge from the faculties or objects. The details of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are fully explained in the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplation).

As for the statement that "it is all due to the ten disciples reaching the Buddha's work," this clarifies that all the disciples have passed through both the Half- and Full-teachings (*śrāvaka* and *bodhisattva* vehicles) in order to achieve the role of assisting and supporting the Dharma.
The King now fully traverses the teachings of one lifetime for the sake of sentient beings;

"reaching the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to entering the secret treasury through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which clarifies that the essential purport of this great sūtra and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* are identical.
Sixth, regarding the production of the fruit in the land of recompense: this again refers to the preceding passage stating that the minds of the two vehicles are the purity of the Bodhisattva.

The intent of the questions and answers in this fascicle is as follows: Therefore, those who refute, those who are refuted, those who hear at the same time, those who hear again later, those who enter the room together, those who enter later, and those who debate from afar—all should enter the Land of Quiescent Light (Sukhāvatī) and abide in their respective fruits of retribution.

However, even if they have entered, they have not yet truly shattered ignorance; they merely abide within the stage of the "Convenient Remaining" (upapadya-śeṣa). Now, as for this current situation...
The *Madhyamāgama* states that because they have already entered the reality (*tattva*), those of great capacity who are reached by the fruit of retribution receive manifest benefit;

whereas for those of small practice, there is only hidden support. Now, speaking according to the intended meaning, it is said that those born in the land of remaining existence (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*)—specifically those who are persons beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) within the various "flavors" (*rasa*)—enter parinirvāṇa immediately and do not reach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, nor do they receive the benefit of non-secrecy.
Therefore, this statement regarding the "seven pure Buddha-lands" is made: purity is precisely the practice of a Bodhisattva. Other scriptural passages contain no such intent;

this [statement] is spoken from the perspective of those who follow provisional practices. If it were spoken from the perspective of those who have not yet revealed their fundamental nature and are shown to be practitioners of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), then because they had previously never established karmic conditions with sentient beings, it was only at the beginning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that they first attained [the path].

Having recorded this, one must further cultivate the practice of the Pure Land. Next, regarding the present citation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, it should be understood that, at first glance, this reveals what is not yet ultimate.
Furthermore, the use of the *Lotus Sūtra* involves two distinct purposes: first, by citing "that which you all practice," it proves the opening of the provisional (*upāya*);

second, by citing "the small desires," it proves the manifestation of the fundamental (*dharmatā*). Therefore, only by interpreting this passage in this manner can it be said that the text is consistent and complete.
Because the Pure Land is thus established, it is known that both Vimalakīrti and his disciples possess a real basis;

therefore, from this point downward, the meaning of "basis and trace" (*honjaku*) is employed to correlate with Vimalakīrti’s basis and thereby conclude the argument. Since ancient times, however, people have treated these matters merely as words of censure and refutation, thereby forever losing the principle of how they accord with the realization of the Buddha-land.
Furthermore, it is not only the case that the meanings of the Buddha and his disciples correspond to the number of kings [in the analogy]; rather, all...
For those who enter the Way, the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are all likewise so. The fundamental intent of the teaching is to cause ordinary beings to practice;

in meaning, this involves the joint transformation of the king and its attendants to bring all minds to perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, each passage concerning "self and others" has the sense of transforming the minds of others, which is similar to purifying the Buddha-lands.
Now, to reflect upon oneself as being the Dharma-body of liberation-knowledge and vision (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) is the true understanding.

Having attained liberation through knowledge and vision, he personally realized the Dharma; this present Vimalakīrti, having completed his realization and attained the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), possesses the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
He reflects that by means of these virtues of liberation, he shall benefit sentient beings—this is because he intends to liberate himself and benefit others.

Regarding the phrase "stills all weariness and affliction" (*kṣapayati sarva-pariśrama-kleśān*): "affliction" (*kleśa*) refers to the defilements, while "matters" (*vastu*) refers to karma; "worldly illness" likewise [refers to these].
One must cease these two matters; now, these two matters represent the cessation of the two matters of afflictions and karma, and of object and wisdom in their mutual correspondence.
Why is this so? Because the essence of these two kinds is precisely the seeds of the two virtues of *prajñā* (wisdom) and liberation.

Now, when the transformation of the seeds of the "Pure Name" (*Vimalakīrti*) is manifested, it is termed "cessation. [The text] asks regarding "the Pure Name," etc., as follows: Question: [Regarding the term] "Pure Name" and so forth... Question: [What is meant by this?]
The meaning of "one who" is simply that one ought to have compassion for others; why then does one think of oneself? The answer is that this indicates the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Within these three virtues, because the object and wisdom are in union, they are called the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā*. However, since liberation has not yet fully manifested within the capacity of those to be converted, one must speak of "mindfulness.
Great Compassion is precisely the manifestation of liberation; because it relies on mindfulness of others, it is described as being "entrusted" to them.
Regarding the three types of the convergence of conditions (*pratyaya-sāmagrī*): within the convergence of two conditions, the convergence of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is added.

Prior to this, in the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṭala*), only two [types] were established. At the beginning of the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the Master Śrīlāta established the convergence of the dharma-realm because it was for the sake of facilitating the explanation and analysis of the chapter and its text.
If it were not so, then disciples and bodhisattvas would merely share a single unconditioned convergence of conditions, and there would be no distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles.

Because it is overly broad, following the ancient tradition, it is divided into three types. If that is so, why does [the text] refute others? The answer is that while the names are the same, the meanings differ, as previously stated.
Regarding "the left side" and so forth: because the worldly convention of the left side emphasizes its functional utility, the current text places it first and addresses it by name.
As for the explanation of "adorned persons" in the latter part of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Tathāgata therein omits the manifestation and enters into the middle.
What is meant by "essence"? It is that the limit itself is the reality; therefore, its withered state is precisely what adorns its flourishing.

The reason flourishing adorns is because it is precisely the withered state. Thus, from the Deer Park until the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the withered and the flourishing were still separated;
the traces of transformation remained distinct. Therefore, those who seek out the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other sutras find that at the time of the *Lotus Sutra*, the three vehicles are [unified].
The assembly of the three [vehicles] is itself one side; only then can it be adorned by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, for all are made to enter therein.

Thus, upon reaching the *Nirvāṇa* [sūtra], it is again manifested to show that the ultimate destination of the entire lifetime of the Buddha's teaching is not something that only becomes capable of being established upon reaching *nirvāṇa*.

There is indeed a reason for citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as "harvesting in autumn and storing in winter. Regarding the phrase "equal in all directions," when one reaches the *Vaipulya* [period], whether great...

If this matter already exists partially within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), yet it is still kept secret and stated that it is not necessarily so, then it must be that what is fixed is actually unfixed.
If one refers to the meaning of the subsequent passage of censure, it is because it accords with the specific text of that censure.

Since it says, "not within the three realms," etc., we know by verification that this is a censure of the Tripitaka (Zàng) from the perspective of the Perfect (Yuán). As for the six losses mentioned previously, they are as follows:

The *Abhidharma* states that these are the "three pairs of distinct [attainments]," namely the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth. (Examine) the *Cheng lun* regarding the two locations where the mind is extinguished when contemplating emptiness.
(Examine) the ten kinds of subtle perceptions as fully explained in the *Zhiguan ji*. The explanation of the name of the attainment of cessation includes refutations, as found in the *Zhiguan ji*.
Next, the lower contemplation of refining and cultivating is clarified, as in the *Fajie cidi chumen*, concerning the first liberation (*vimokṣa*) and the two spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Regarding those who possess internal perception of form while externally perceiving forms—whether few or many—these are divided into two, three, and four [categories], making two types of *abhibhvāyatana* (bases of mastery).
In the text, the case of "having no internal perception of form while externally perceiving forms—whether few or many"—is omitted; this is also divided into two.

The remaining four *abhibhvāyatanas* are identical to the four colored objects among the eight *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities) within the pure liberations (*śubhavimokṣa*). This is explained in detail in the *Chanmen* (Dhyāna Gate), which states: "Eight."
Regarding the "all-pervasive bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*): there are eighteen such bases in total, as ten exist within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and eight within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Here, we do not discuss [the latter] because they consist of the two all-pervasive bases of space and consciousness. Now, to clarify the mutual generation of the five flavors based on the lower [stages], we temporarily rely on the five dhyānas to illustrate these five flavors;
the wise should understand that this refers to the text on the "Wish-Knowledge" (*praṇidhijñāna*) and the "Culmination Dhyāna" (*mūrdhadhyāna*).
This is a further elaboration. Because this *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from aspiration) and dhyāna abide above all other dhyānas, it is called the "summit" (*mūrdhan*).

It receives its name because within that dhyāna one can give rise to various aspirations, wisdoms, and so forth. Regarding the eighteen transformations, they are as explained in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-ṭīkā*.
As for the "ultimate summit of all dhyānas," if one relies upon contemplation and the like to cultivate them to their full extent, they all—
Regarding the question, "Why is it called 'attaining the summit' (*mūrdhan*)? and so forth: if there were only the fundamental [dhyānas], this question would not arise.

Furthermore, by adding the four pairs such as "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) to the fundamental [dhyānas], they become five. Since the "liberations" (*vimokṣa*) and so forth all rely on the distinct stages of dhyāna, why are the four pairs such as "contemplation" established separately?
The intended meaning of the answer is simply that one perfumes the fundamental [dhyānas] with contemplation and so forth, thereby refining the fundamentals. As for the "three pairs":
All these are names within the essence of *parinirvāṇa* itself; they still seem to overlap with the Lesser Vehicle. Why?

For instance, Śāriputra also said that when he entered the extinction-concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he was not within the three realms, yet he manifested in the mind; later, upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, he did not manifest in the body.

Why, then, does [Vimalakīrti] reprimand him for "manifesting both body and mind"? However, Vimalakīrti’s intention in his reprimand concerns the present; had he been speaking of the future, it would have applied to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If [the Buddha] has also entered cessation, why is it that only Śāriputra—and not the other two pairs or the single one—is beyond the range of his vision and hearing?
Next, regarding the application of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the text directly refutes the concentration entered by Śāriputra as being incapable of such [insight].
Regarding the other two pairs, this is a critique of their lack of wisdom within concentration; for the second pair, it further combines the previous critique of their concentration with this point.

The next pair and single [term] mostly belong to wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, although the name "pair of cause and effect" is established only upon reaching the third [stage], the preceding two pairs both refer to the fruit (*phala*).
The reason the text below again speaks of the "fruit" is to contrast it with the cause;
even though the cause is established, it is done so for the sake of achieving the fruit. Because this rebuke of Śāriputra was not directed toward others, it is categorized solely within the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the fruit of realization, because the small fruits are criticized, the five dharmas—excluding the cause—are first directly cited as Bodhisattvas;
subsequently, the Dharmakāya Bodhisattva is again raised to contrast and refute the small fruits by means of those who have attained partial realization.

This culminates in the criticism of Maudgalyāyana’s conditions regarding the eight hundred [Arhats], wherein all the causal dharmas of the three teachings are used for the refutation below, extending down to the eight persons; this is where the text belongs.

Regarding the phrase "one whose body is like wood or stone," although such a person is like wood or stone, they possess this body; and although they are like extinguished ashes, they have a solemn vow.
Therefore, they are all called "those who possess a body. Why must one do so for the sake of seeking fame and profit?

Because manifesting this appearance is entirely similar to manifesting a sign, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) employs it as a means of censure. As for the phrase "this is the inconceivable," [the text] asks: "What is this?"

Question: True *pratisaṃlayanā* (seated meditation) is inconceivable; why then is it said "up to and including" (*yāvat*)? Answer: This is because Śāriputra was rebuked for his attachment to meditative concentration based on phenomena (*dharmasthiti-samādhi*).
First, he was led to enter the nine grades of *dhyāna* with the mind of Buddha-wisdom; this is the *dhyāna* of the Separate Teaching (*bipartite-teaching*).

Next, those who are the same as the Two Vehicles [were led to] enter the concentrations of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* [teachings]; this refers to the person of the Separate Teaching entering these concentrations. Finally, within the inconceivable [state], he transcends one grade.
Because all things are provisionally manifested, it is said: "even while remaining in desire, one practices dhyāna.
This statement is made with reference to the true meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) at the stage of fruition; its intent is to cause entry into the inconceivable provisional.

Therefore, it says "remaining in desire," not because ordinary people in a state of desire possess dhyāna. The present meaning is that Māra originally uses desire to disturb worldly people, and since...
Because they take the realm of Māra as the work of a Buddha, when Māra beholds them, his mind becomes distressed and confused.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva below does not manifest the contemplative practices of body and mind for those who rely on him.

Moreover, regarding the Dharma-body below, he uses the causal vehicle of non-arising to rebuke those who possess partial fruits; since both Great and Small Vehicles share the fruit, why do you remain within the three realms?
If you claim that the present body and mind are identical to the principle (*tattva*), I fear you are pushing toward a grand result;
therefore, I shall challenge you with the inconceivable nature of phenomena and principle. Since neither phenomena nor principle accord with what you assert, they are useless to yourself.

As for the question of why one would attain this samādhi while neglecting other modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*)—what benefit is there for others? Such claims of uselessness were previously refuted by the critique of their lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If one merely censures that which is useless in essence, how does this differ from [censuring] non-existence? Now, by censuring the useless, one effectively censures both [the unwholesome and the neutral];

thus, the various unwholesome actions performed through the three karmas are simply termed "unwholesome," whereas when they are conjoined with the three poisons, they are then termed "roots of the unwholesome.
The wholesome and the roots of the wholesome may be understood accordingly; all of these exist within the realm of conditioned existence (*dhātu*).
Therefore it is said: "When ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) question about the arising of the three karmas, they necessarily involve the three poisons (triviṣa).

How can there be an 'arising' that is pervasive yet not called a 'root' (mūla), while waiting for a distinct arising before it is named a root? Answer: The meaning of a "root" is its capacity to produce future lives.

That which arises in a general or pervasive manner coexists with the three poisons but does not attract retribution in a future existence; thus, it is not called a "root. Taken as a whole, this is the explanation.
Furthermore, just as ordinary beings accomplish their tasks through the three types of tainted karma (*sāsrava-karman*), this is the external function beyond the fixed dharma of the Bodhisattva;

therefore, there is no need to abandon [the world] to lead sentient beings to the Pure Land. Thus, one should know that among the six dharmas, possessing even a single one is sufficient to benefit living beings.
For the sake of benefiting living beings, one must take up the Pure Land in its entirety, as described in the preceding two points.
Regarding the nineteen matters that should now be treated as equal: among the four propositions, the third is that which is censured and the fourth is that which censures;

the remaining two propositions follow from these characteristics. Thus, when the Buddha addressed Subhadra and others with the "lion’s roar," he spoke of the Buddha-nature and the Eightfold Noble Path.
As for being "immovable" and "not practicing," this is because of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which entails the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Because of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), there are also the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); because these are supplemented by eighty-eight [afflictions], it is said that they are "immovable.

Regarding the cultivation of the four "withered" applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, this is the general path of practice as detailed in the seventh fascicle of the *Śamathavipaśyanā* (Mo-ho chih-kuan) and its commentary.

If one possesses the view of self and the view of existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one is fully possessed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The aggregates are the objects of contemplation in the Four Teachings. As for the seventy-three types of persons...

Regarding the aforementioned eight stages, each has nine grades; thus, there are seventy-two persons (8 × 9 = 72), to which one person from the desire realm who possesses full afflictions is added, totaling seventy-three persons (check the *Abhidharmakośa*).
As for the "eight masteries," as stated in the *Zhiguan ji*, they enter the intermediate stage through two types of abandonment.

Regarding the "distinct teaching" (*biejiao*), this refers to the beginning of the ten abodes of the distinct practitioner, who merely employs the teachings of the Two Vehicles and is unable [to proceed further].
Using afflictions as the work of a Buddha refers precisely to the stage of the first dwelling (*prathamabhūmi*).
Although it is said that "he enters [samādhi]," one should rather say that nirvāṇa is fundamentally unmoving; thus, this metaphor is applied subtly.

For this reason, Śāriputra not only possesses the wisdom of non-abiding, but also enters the samādhi of non-wisdom. It is for this meaning that he was rebuked from within samādhi, and it is also because of this.
Regarding the statement that Śāriputra’s wisdom was absent from meditative concentration and that he entered the cessation-attainment of non-wisdom, yet manifested his physical form:
this is because he manifested the appearance of a body by entering [the attainment] as a person who has attained the fruit; thus, he is criticized entirely on account of the fruit.

In the tenth fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, it is stated that [the Buddha] next commanded Maudgalyāyana to respond to the layman (*gṛhapati*). This was done entirely by means of reprimand based on causes, and furthermore, by means of reprimand through the side of the teaching.
Since all lay followers are possessed of the conditioned accumulation of conditions (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudaya*), it was necessary to employ both the general and the specific approaches.
Yuan [comments]: If this were addressed solely to Maudgalyāyana, it would be a case of rebuking the Small Vehicle with the Three Vehicles. Furthermore, as for why he next summons Maudgalyāyana:
since his wisdom is not far removed from that of Śāriputra, and he is also capable of attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet this alone is insufficient to manifest his excellence.

As the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states: "The ancient seers delighted in this; those who seek its ultimate principle deeply shall proceed from here to the meaning of benefiting others. This is found in various texts.
This is so; because it exhorts one not to forget the root, it is said that one must seek deeply downward, and all subsequent sections are likewise thus.

Śāriputra was also like this. Regarding the gradual manifestation, "gradual teaching" refers to the second stage of flourishing. As for the contrast between the "Half" and the "Full": that which is refuted is fixed as the Half, while that which can censure it is the Full.
Within the gateway [of the Full], although the numbers three, two, or one are not fixed, all three are called "Full," and it is by virtue of this that [the realization] is attained.
Names are mutually dependent; it is said that those who preach the characteristics of the Lesser Dharma for the sake of those with Great capacities provide only the slightest benefit.
Because both [parties] lose their way, the preceding section generally censures them by saying, "one should not be like those people who speak.

Here, the character "dāng" (當) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*), the intent being to clarify that what is being said is improper. If it were pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*), it could only be used to explain the meaning [of the term].
This is precisely what was stated as being unreasonable. If one reads the scriptures regularly, one must rely on the level tone (*ping sheng*);

how much more so when employing the departing tone (*qu sheng*), for the character "dang" (應) must serve as the final syllable of the phrase, and thus it is not permissible [to use it otherwise]. Regarding the brief differentiation of the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) into their distinct categories:

first, there is a brief indication of their differences; next, the preceding section clarifies them; and below, the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles are analyzed. As for "If it is... and so forth: 1. Briefly indicating the differences. 2. Preceding clarification of the distinctions. 3. Below, the analysis of the characteristics of the Great and Small Vehicles. 4. If it is... and so forth.

Clarifying the differences in how the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and the Mahāyāna enter the Dharma; the four purities are named below as a conclusion regarding their respective applications. Within the section on "Discriminating Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇavibhaṅga*), there are two parts:

first, the Lesser Vehicle, and second, the Mahāyāna. Within the first part (the Lesser Vehicle), there are five sections: first, a brief citation of the differences between the two emptinesses (*śūnyatā*);

second, based on the *Āgamas*, the following clarifies how various sūtras and śāstras employ emptiness to varying degrees to establish the three types of emptiness; third, "If there is a person... and so forth, which provides an explanation.

1. "Equality and Emptiness" (Section 4): This section refutes the two lower vehicles and unifies them [with the Mahāyāna]. 2. "Although... (Section 5): This concludes by returning to the fundamental school.
Next, the refutation of the Mahāyāna: Within this, first the skillful and the clumsy are contrasted; next, "These three... correctly clarifies the characteristics of the Mahāyāna;

third, regarding the differences in entering the Dharma, first the Hīnayāna, then the Mahāyāna; within the Mahāyāna, first the characteristics of the Mahāyāna are correctly clarified, followed by "If one relies on... [the commentary continues].

The lower section clarifies that "penetration" refers to the four purities; this concludes the brief analysis of the text regarding the application of the conclusion. Next, we shall briefly interpret the initial minor and middle sections.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Who undergoes old age and death," if one speaks of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), the word "non-" (*a-* or *na-*) must be added—meaning "there is no such thing as old age and death" and "there is no one who undergoes old age and death"—as is fully detailed in the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of the Cessation and Contemplation). Next, within the section on mutual comparison, there are two parts... [first].
The Dharma is likened to the absence of a fist, which is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); the absence of fingers is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The absence of emptiness itself is the emptiness of equality (*samatā-śūnyatā*). The character "expedient" (*quán*) in the text is likely an error for "equality. Regarding the two preceding types of emptiness as skillful means:
it is by entering the emptiness of phenomena that one enters true emptiness, which is then termed "equality. One should know that the very emptiness realized is designated as equality. If...
Regarding the phrase "the Mahāyāna teachings, etc.," it refers to the three names being without distinction because the three are identical to the one; therefore, there is only the name.

Since this is skillful emptiness, it is itself the True and the Middle, and thus they should not be explained separately. As for the phrase "the three are the Middle," it does not mean that all things are necessarily the Middle;

rather, it means that this conventional reality (saṃvṛti) extends to the Middle. Therefore, the commentary states: "All extend to the Dharma-nature. Regarding the passage beginning with "If one receives and follows [the teachings]," it clarifies... [text truncated].
Regarding "penetrating through penetration": those of dull faculties do not see the dharma-nature beforehand, as they abide only in the partial truth;
therefore it is said that these bodhisattvas of superior faculties penetrate up to the dharma-nature, meaning they are those of middling-sharp capacity among bodhisattvas.
Thus, because all subsequent passages penetrate the dharma-nature, it says that one "sees the middle way. If you do not believe in the meaning of the shared emptiness, I shall now ask you:

He said: "As the sutras state, 'Dharmas have no sentient beings, for they are free from the defilements of sentient beings,' and so forth—is this not precisely the absence of the four [concepts] of sentient beings, self, person, and life-span?
Since the followers of the Two Vehicles have already abandoned these four dharmas, why are they still used here to criticize the Lesser Vehicle?

If the Lesser is criticized by means of the Great, one must distinguish between them; in this context, it should be said that while the objects abandoned are no different, the agents of abandonment differ."

The wisdom of emptiness distinguishes the intent of our own school [the Tiantai], which is able to transcend the three [vehicles]. One should know that while the "common" and the "provisional" share what is to be transcended, they differ;

whereas the "distinct" and the "perfect" are able to transcend it eternally and fundamentally. Regarding the interpretation of these meanings, all must be complete; yet when categorized according to the three teachings, the conventional is the same while the true differs, and the essence of the truth must be distinguished.

Now, this commentary follows the superior [perspective] and provisionally explains it from the standpoint of the Perfect Teaching, where the mind-dharmas and the dharma-nature—such as the words [used here]—are still [to be further analyzed].
This applies to all three emptinesses; everything is thus. Only when one has correctly grasped this principle can it be said that one has skillfully digested the three emptinesses.

Furthermore, regarding all the phrases listed in the sutra text—specifically the term "all dharmas" (sarvadharma) and the various names for "the nature of dharmas" (dharmatā) within the commentary—one must distinguish them so that they fully possess the three truths.
If they were merely "perfectly round" (yuan), then there would be no objects outside the mind, and the one would subsume the one.
By all means, do not fail to achieve thorough integration; here we simultaneously refute conventional meanings and integrate the provisional with the ultimate.

Furthermore, one should know that what is to be observed by a beginner does not transcend all mental phenomena within the realm. Because they are identical, their meanings are intermingled despite their apparent differences. Regarding the question on the emptiness of sentient beings and so forth:

this is based on the general [teaching], specifically addressing the emptiness of persons. Within the question-and-answer section, both cases concern those of sharp faculties among the general [practitioners].

In the Middle Way Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the interpretation of the meaning of the emptiness of sentient beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) cites sūtras to substantiate this meaning; all cases are thus.
Only by subtly grasping the profound intent of the three truths within the seven stages can one fully comprehend the preceding and succeeding passages of the sūtra.

However, according to the Perfect Interpretation, if even sentient beings themselves are identical to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), how much more so must the emptiness of sentient beings be so? Therefore, it causes all [beings] to proceed toward [enlightenment].

Regarding my subsequent citation of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, I cited six dharmas to pose a question; that [the self] is neither identical to nor separate from them has already been established in other passages.
Within this context, one merely takes up the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and thus the citation of the sixty-two views constitutes the answer.
Since the passages from the preceding sections have already been analyzed and resolved, why raise this doubt again? As it is said: "The names of all three are together."
Because it immediately enters into the ultimate reality (*tattva*), the subsequent passage is divided into those of inferior and superior faculties.

The inferior faculty refers to the ultimate reality; the superior faculty refers to the middle. The middle proceeds from the profound to the shallow; because the profound is not lost when in the shallow, the shallow is concealed by following the profound.

Thus, a single sound universally reaches all. Furthermore, according to the principles of the Sautrāntika school, one should adapt to the capacities of beings. Following the manifest text of the sūtra, for the time being, we follow the universal [application].
The commentary explains that as it is said, "In the Dharma there are no sentient beings," the teachings of the three vehicles are all alike in having no sentient beings;
yet, because the application of wisdom differs, they are established as three distinct types. Thus, the terms "Dharmatā," "True Wisdom," and "Expedient Means" are all universally applicable;

however, they are illustrated by the character *ī* (which is both unified and differentiated). Furthermore, one must know that from this point onward, within each of the subsequent phrases concerning expedient means and wisdom, both [aspects] are fully present.
Regarding the statement "the mind itself acts and transforms others," and the subsequent phrases which all speak of "the mind and all dharmas":

if these phrases are applied across the mind and in relation to dharmas, who is there to perceive them? Is the single phrase "do not think of one's own conduct" merely relying on the literal text of the Dharma?
As for the "characteristics of the mind" mentioned in the case of Upāli, the following text specifically concerns the mind that commits offenses, which is fundamentally without defilement.
Just as Upāli attained liberation through the Lesser Vehicle, does he not see that the mind is liberated from the thought of transgression?

Because the nature of the mind is not distinct [from the mind itself], all things are, from the perspective of their rational essence (*dharmatā*), without stain. Just as the Supreme Heavenly King cites "emptiness of self-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) to prove that the principle-dharma is free from the stains of sentient beings, and cites "separation from self-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-vivikta*) to prove that within the principle there is separation from the stains of sentient beings—all of these refer to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

It is further stated that within the subsequent section on "actual wisdom" (*bhūtaprajñā*), the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) is first cited because it is by virtue of the non-existence of this nature that wisdom brings about non-existence.
Although the nature is non-existent, the fact that something still persists is precisely due to the absence of wisdom; [the mind] cannot be absent of itself.

However, when one speaks of "dharmas" and does not speak of "mind," since mind and dharmas mutually encompass one another, citing one serves as a general principle that applies to all subsequent phrases.

"All are thus" refers to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) reaching its state of defilement; herein two factors are present: first, a total lack of understanding that within the ultimate truth there is no self;
second, even if one understands the ultimate truth, one does not know the middle way. Because of these teachings, I still possess defilement;

because of this defilement, they are collectively termed "erroneous conceptualization. Next, from "if one descends" onwards, it clarifies the wisdom that accords with reality, which is non-conceptual and in accord with principle.

All subsequent phrases are entirely like this; they follow the pattern of the preceding "agent. The first two [phrases] are easily categorized within the context of skillful means (*upāya*), as all possess both self and other—like the letter *i* and so forth—and all subsequent ones are likewise. This is not the same as the ordinary person who has reached the limit of severance;
this is stated for the sake of convenience regarding these two extremes. In full, it should be said that they are not the same as those who possess the seven kinds of skillful means.

This is not merely that the "perfect" [nature] cannot be further explained; the subsequent examples are likewise so. Next, regarding the eight sections that correctly clarify the entry into emptiness by means of the dharmas that constitute the essence:

since it was previously clarified that those who enter the Mahāyāna gate are themselves the dharmas and should not be spoken of separately, the statement "the essence of dharmas" applies generally to both persons and dharmas. Therefore, concerning the person who is the object of emptification—

Because the Dharma is explained separately in relation to that which is empty, it is stated again; thus, within the emptiness of the object, the emptiness of persons refers only to sentient beings, life-span, and so forth.
That very essence which is the emptiness of the subject is eternally quiescent, with all marks perpetually extinguished—this is called the emptiness of dharmas.
If this were not stated, how could one know that the same applies to what follows? Let the reader embody this and the practitioner examine it, so as to dissolve [all attachments].
Regarding the purport of this teaching, it is the same throughout its preceding and succeeding sections; one should repeatedly harmonize these parts so as not to lose sight of the essential meaning.
As for the "ten marks," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that they consist of the marks of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, birth, abiding, change, extinction, and male and female.
However, merely being free from these ten is not sufficient to manifest the virtues of the Great Nirvāṇa. Yet, the intent of the sutra is to say that within the Great Nirvāṇa, these do not exist.
These ten characteristics do not merely refute the discriminative consciousness of those who claim to have attained the wisdom-consciousness of Great Nirvāṇa;
they also refute discriminative wisdom itself. Since they currently pertain precisely to the two characteristics of emptiness and conventionality, they are termed "discriminative.

Therefore, according to the Middle Way principle, the non-discriminative object cannot possibly be an object of perception for wisdom-consciousness. Question: Is there not also a single wisdom that perceives [both]?

Question: Regarding the many objects—such as when conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) illuminates the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the middle (*madhyama*), or when the ultimate and the conventional mutually and alternately illuminate one another—what is the principle behind this?

Answer: If we discuss the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of entering the realm of emptiness, then a single instance of the conventional is opposed to the three instances of the ultimate, mutually illuminating and alternatingly illuminating;
however, this is not what is being discussed here. As for the statement "there is no teaching of dharmas" and so forth, it is because all verbal expressions arise from cognition (*buddhi*).

When observing arising, all words are derived from vitarka and vicāra; they are both devoid of the nature of dharmas, for the nature of dharmas—both the speaker and the spoken—is fundamentally non-existent.

When true wisdom illuminates them, they are thus rendered free from attachment through skillful means. This does not pertain to the sixth, seventh, or eighth consciousnesses, as "consciousness" (vijñāna) is defined by discrimination;
therefore, it is said that all [words] are non-existent. Question: Why not also say that the five consciousnesses are non-existent? Answer: Because of the sense organs (*indriya*).
The object cannot be absent; moreover, since the first five [consciousnesses] are unable to discern phenomena, the fault lies with the sixth and seventh, so what crime has the fifth committed?
If that is so, what loss is there for the eighth? Answer: Because it is neutral (*avyākṛta*), retributive (*vipāka*), and contains defilements (*saṃkleśa*);
taken as a whole, it belongs to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. If that is so, why are the first five not listed as belonging to saṃsāra? Answer: Because one must observe their respective objects.
If that is so, why is it said that the sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses] are also objects of contemplation? The answer is:

when we say they do not exist, it is because the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) does not exist [as a substantial entity]; for the principle of *dharmatā* cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known.

If that is so, why do you not say that eye-consciousness and the others do not exist? The answer is: for the time being, they must be established [as conventional realities], as the subsequent text also states that "phenomena transcend the eye and so forth."
The nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is precisely that which cannot be absent; such is the principle of its nature, and it must necessarily conform to this.
Regarding the seven sections below and the various phrases, there should still be nine sections in total as they proceed.

That which "seems equal" is so because it accords with non-reliance (*apratītya*), and because it is identical to the *dharmatā* and identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); these expressions are entirely equal. However, the force of these various phrases is like "detachment."
Good and ugly, as well as "passing before the eyes" and so forth, are also intended to be the same as the previously mentioned "dharmas arising" and the two types of emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

because they encompass both the progressive and regressive [perspectives], they are for the time being described as "resembling" [emptiness]. Furthermore, because they are not the same as the previous seven [categories], it is said that they do not belong to causes and conditions and have no coming or going.

Since the three types of emptiness are one in essence, they may be so described; moreover, since "equal emptiness" and "dharma-emptiness" are intermingled, this "intermingling" also implies inclusion.
The reason for using synonymous terms is that each phrase can be explained simultaneously; thus it is called "mixed" (*miśra*), not because it is a mere conjunction of various elements.

One should know that the characteristics of arising phenomena appear as if they depend on something else; therefore, by means of equality, one repeatedly severs them. The initial statement that there is "no mutual dependence" means that even "non-existence" is a severance, for it severs that very dependence.
Thus, one severs from the perspective of the mind rather than severing from the perspective of phenomena; since the severance of phenomena is inexhaustible, the severance [itself] is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, regarding the non-interruption of the mind: according to the ultimate reality (*tattva*), this reality is the *dharmatā*.
Since the *dharmatā* is fundamentally non-existent, there is not even "non-interruption" to be found; how, then, could there be the delusion of "non-interruption" based on mutual dependence?

When wisdom accords with the *dharmatā*, it is then termed "cessation. Therefore, even the *dharmatā* ceases within that cessation. Because there is still something remaining within the principle of equality, one attains the second [stage].
Emptiness is precisely what is called "equality. That which is said to "exist" is intended by the meaning [of the teaching] to bring about cessation; there is necessarily nothing that exists.
One should know that equality itself lacks the name "equality"; it is emptiness that is called equality. If this were not so, why would it be called the Gate of the Mahāyāna?

Since the three types of emptiness are simultaneous, one wishes to manifest their functional capacity as being without differentiation. Therefore, by listing that which "exists," one manifests that which "does not exist," desiring to attain equality.
Since even the dharmas that arise equally do not exist, how could there further remain the view of equality? Therefore, it is said that there is simply no equality.
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka master below further cites the Small Tripitaka to contrast it with the Great Tripitaka; even if there were equality, it would ultimately possess no distinct principle.

Moreover, when the two kinds of emptiness are established according to the Lesser Vehicle teachings, they have not yet attained equality; how much less so when one further cultivates the "emptiness of emptiness" regarding that equality!

Therefore, the three types of emptiness in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ. Regarding the cessation of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the mind: when the cognitive hindrance is present, it still belongs to the realm of relative dependence;

both hindrances are merely the wisdom of emptiness and the provisional. Although one reaches the stage of the first *vihāra* (abode) by means of the shared vehicle, the cognitive hindrance must be extinguished;

this is not because of the six causes, nor does it fall under the four conditions. A brief explanation is as found in the *Zhiguan ji* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. If one wishes for a rough [explanation]...
Regarding the knowledge of their names: "old" refers to the *kṛta* (produced), *sahabhū* (co-existent), *svabhāva* (self-nature), *sarvatraga* (pervasive), and *vipāka* (maturation);

"new" refers to the *kāraṇa* (efficient cause), *sahabhū* (co-existent), *sabhāga* (homogeneous), *saṃprayukta* (associated), *sarvatraga* (pervasive), and *vipāka* (maturation). Regarding the four conditions:

"old" refers to the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition), *anantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition), *ālambana-pratyaya* (object condition), and *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition); "new" refers to the *ālambana-pratyaya* as the *ālambana* (objective support).

The conditions of object (*ālambana*) and immediate succession (*samanantara*) are called the "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*). The remaining two [conditions] share the same name as the "great body," which is also the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

they simply do not arise from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), because that which exists as a causal phenomenon must necessarily belong to conditions, and because causes and conditions are necessarily conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding the "twelve," etc., the four conditions, the six causes, and so forth, are all birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and birth-and-death is itself the three [natures].

The three paths are identical to the three virtues, and the three virtues are the dharma-nature (dharmatā). Outside of the three virtues, there are no further three paths; thus, it may be said that they are "identical.
This is because the twelve links of dependent origination share the same function, and these twelve are likewise merely four or six [groups].

Therefore, one knows that this is merely a matter of differentiating and combining the explanation. For instance, ignorance (*avidyā*) is precisely the capacity for penetration within the category of formations (*saṃskāra*). Thus...

Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), its activity necessarily consists of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) which are co-existent (*sahabhū*). Within this activity, the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) are likewise homogeneous.

Among ignorance and formations, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) act together and experience the results together; that which is produced must necessarily be a concomitant factor (*sahabhū-aṅga*), and this activity necessarily brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of consciousness and so forth.

This activity necessarily involves the five categories of pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*). As for the four conditions (*pratyaya*), the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "If [the condition] increases..."
The preceding [discussion] concerning the nature of the five causes as acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) can be understood by analogy with the explanation of the six causes.

However, in the commentary (*śāstra*), regarding the acting cause (*kāritra-hetu*) and the dominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*) within the category of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is stated that they are identical to "mutual dependence" (*apekṣā*). This is because, within the dominant cause, both the powerful and the powerless are capable of bringing about a result;

since the agent and the object are distinct in relation to that which is produced, they are termed "mutually dependent. How much more so, then, is this the case for the relationship between the producer and the produced?

Within the middle [nature], there are such things as length, shortness, largeness, smallness, and so forth; yet within the nature of the self and dharmas (*ātma-dharma-tathatā*), these things do not exist at all.

Therefore, it is refuted by means of equality. Regarding the phrase "because it is precise," in this skillful means, one merely uses the principle of responding to objects according to conditions to dismantle [false views].
If worldly phenomena belong to causes and conditions, they can only be established when the provisional cause meets with conditions, just as clay [requires water and a potter].
Just as the formation of tiles necessarily depends on the condition of fire, and the turning of earth into mud necessarily depends on water, so too does one dharma enter all dharmas.
Regarding the principle that "all dharmas possess peace and bliss," this refers to the meaning of being inherently present (*hon-yū*).

Since it is said that they mutually enter because their characteristics are inherently present, the further mention of "mutual entry" demonstrates the inclusion of characteristics and shows that these characteristics reside within the dharmas; thus, the dharma is itself the characteristic.

Regarding the phrase "the nature and so forth": although phenomena are fundamentally [interfused], one must necessarily enter them through actual wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*) before the nature of the mutual interpenetration of all phenomena can be realized.
When principle and wisdom are unified, this is precisely the expedient means (*upāya*) of the three mysteries responding to capacities; therefore, it is said that one should "enter" the phenomena.

That "phenomena are themselves wisdom" means that object and wisdom are non-dual. However, even within the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) has already been refuted.
To "attain entry into the ultimate truth" (paramārtha-satya) is now termed "dharma-nature" (dharmatā), because it does not belong to causes and conditions; thus, there is a slight distinction.

If they were not different, then within dharma-nature, suchness (tathatā) is one, and there is no second dharma; as for "abiding in the limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi) and so forth, since dharma-nature, the limit of reality, and suchness differ in name but are identical in meaning, they are free from the four extremes.
This principle also applies to the three [natures], yet in the present text, the intention is focused primarily on one.

To briefly summarize the integration of principle and wisdom, one should speak of the four teachings and so forth. Because [the nature of reality] is inherently complete (*liju*), it subsequently arises universally;

"not depending on the six sense objects" means that "depending" (*yi*) refers to attachment. If this is so, do those of the Tripitaka Hīnayāna not attach to the six sense objects? The answer is: they possess [attachment], yet they claim to be free from it;

however, their "freedom" is still identical to attachment, because they are attached to the "non-existence" within the two [existence and non-existence]. When the sense objects are separated from the two [extremes of existence and non-existence], it is called "non-attachment."
It is quite different from the meaning of being bound by chains of gold or iron; in the Mahāyāna, both are abandoned. This is because one perceives the true and conventional *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding the statement that "phenomena have no going or coming," a question is raised: "If they do not abide, this is also going and coming;
how can you explain 'no going or coming'? The answer is: "Non-abiding means non-going. Since there is no abiding and no going, there is nothing [to be called] going or coming."
Because going and coming [are negated], one can thereby explain the absence of going and coming. The meaning clarifies that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) does not abide in any partiality;

thus it is said that "non-abiding" distinguishes it from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which involve going and abiding. Regarding the *Śrāvaka Sūtras* reaching the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) and so forth:

"emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) refers to emptiness and non-self; "signlessness" (*animitta*) refers to cessation; and "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*) refers to the remaining ten [aspects] based on the truths, each being threefold.
