Because it is immutable, it can produce; because it can produce, it is immutable. These two—lineage and nature—are entirely without beginning or end, existing eternally from time immemorial;
they are sufficient as a reliable basis for faith. The question, "If Buddha-nature has three kinds," etc., intends to clarify that they are the same as previously explained.
Although the preceding text, in response to a different question, stated that the Path is itself the Nature (*dhātu*), this was merely a general explanation of the title of the chapter.

Now, regarding the question within the chapter as to whether there are three kinds of "seeds" (*bīja*), the intent of the answer can be understood. As for the characteristics and essential nature of these seeds:

here, four names are listed; though the names differ, their meaning is the same. This present "seed-nature" (*gotra*) is intended to be eternally distinct [from other categories], such that its characteristics are manifested externally and even with... [the former].

The nature is identical to the seed; arising from within accords with its nature. Regarding the question that "seed" takes the capacity to produce as its meaning, since all Buddhas take these two meanings as fundamental, one should know that *tathatā*, the *dharmadhātu*, and the secret treasury of *dharmatā* are all to be addressed by way of the "seed.

In the answer, the meanings of the "enabling condition" (*pariniṣpanna*) and the "contributing condition" (*parikalpita*) are not taken as the meaning of "seed"; rather, it is only when seeking from within that [the seed is realized].
Thus, by analogy, that which emerges from the correct nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is also called a "seed"; therefore, we know that the three paths are able to produce the three natures.
Why must one insist that seeds grow only externally? Furthermore, the term "seed" should also be explained by analogy, as is fully clarified in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
It is not only the case that the primary seed is not the cause; the same applies to karma and afflictions, which serve as the conditions for the "perceiving" and "discerning" [causes].

This is because, as will be clarified below, since the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*) exists, it can also be termed "nature" (*prakṛti*) by way of contrast with the "correct object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the "conditioning cause" (*vijñāna-pratyaya*).

Thus, all three names—seed, cause, and nature—share the same meaning despite having different names; this must be well-considered. Since the mind and its objects are not distinct, the principles naturally coincide.
The answer states: "If it is as you have asked, then it is a universal meaning. Universal and particular are merely... [the text ends here].
The meaning of separation and union is fully explained in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) and the *Fenbie buer men* (Discrimination of the Non-dual Gate).

Regarding the statement that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the dharma-nature possess ignorance and unwholesomeness: "ignorance" refers to delusion; "unwholesome" refers to karma; and the "neutral" five aggregates are originally named the dharma-nature.

It is because these aggregates are falsely conceived through the addition of delusion and karma that confusion arises; yet, since the dharma-nature is inherently pure from the beginning, it causes the three [kinds of phenomena]... [to manifest].

When various delusions arise, they are all delusions; yet the principle is fundamentally pure. Because cause and effect are explained in contrast to one another, it is said that when ignorance and unwholesomeness exist, they constitute birth and death, whereas their transformation is called purity.
Regarding the masters of the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* and others who claim that the seven consciousnesses are a single entity:

this is a conceptual construction of difference. Based on this view, they hold that consciousness is the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*). From the perspective of its revealing function, it is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*); from the perspective of delusion, it is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). Thus spoke the ancients.
It is not by mutual attachment that disputes arise; the same applies to the six consciousnesses acting as conditions. Regarding the contemplation of the mind:

although previously it was discussed in terms of the twelve links of dependent origination and the three realms of suffering within the ten dharma-realms, it was not stated that these constitute the object of contemplation.

Now, it is said that the ten realms and the twelve links of dependent origination are but a single thought-moment. How does this differ from what was stated before? Fearing that people might not understand, this is explained separately.
Regarding these preceding matters, there is no different path: with a single mind and a single color, everything is none other than the ten realms as emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle.
How much more so when the mind is raised—delusion itself becomes wisdom, and as one turns according to contemplation, one spontaneously attains liberation, which is termed "ultimate.
Furthermore, if we discuss suffering as the primary object, it is also evident upon karma and delusion; thus, the three meanings of suffering, form, and mind are fully present.
This is because when the three virtues are fully realized and not obscured, one can penetrate to the ultimate; thus it is called "unobstructed.

It is like the letter *i*, for both cause and effect, as well as phenomena and principle, together form the analogy of the *i*. According to what others have explained, if the principle were one, then the two—the cultivation of causes and the attainment of effects—would both fail to constitute the *i*.
Principles such as permanence and impermanence must be clearly expounded; if awakening reaches the state of a Tathāgata, then indeed [it is so].
These three paths all possess the meaning of being able to produce the conditions and the objects of cognition (*ālambana*).

Regarding the meaning of being able to produce the conditions and objects of cognition, having already established it as before, one should further inquire: Is it not the case that when the seeds proceed toward their own respective merits, they are spoken of in terms of their own activity?
It is merely by means of the two wisdoms (*jñāna*) that the Dharma-body and the function of liberation can be manifested; the two wisdoms are the provisional and the ultimate *prajñā*.

The objective realm is not termed "merit," while the two wisdoms that transform others are termed "one skillful means. Regarding Vimalakīrti’s statement "equal," one should know that the meaning of the response possesses two aspects:
first, emerging from the conventional (出假); second, being identical to principle (即理). If one does not emerge from the conventional, there is no way to manifest the universal characteristic (通相);

if one does not abide in identity with principle, there is no way to manifest the universality of principle within the conventional. This is because the subsequent [sections] depend upon the preceding.

Having gone through the seven sections and thoroughly understood their meaning, one may then state the great purport of this chapter’s text. Furthermore, below, there is a further detailed analysis concerning the "provisional" (jia) being a non-path (*amārga*).

This refers specifically to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) and points out that provisional wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth are non-paths. Regarding the results of the fivefold three miserable realms (*trividha-durgati*):
Question: As for the result of the Avīci hell, why is it said to induce rebirth as a hungry ghost or an animal, when you generally refer to them collectively as the "three miserable realms"?
The other two are the attendants of the immediate [retributions], for at the time of creating the cause, they naturally follow along;
thus, karma leading to the two evil destinies may also have other retributions that extend to the other two. This clarifies the gateway through which Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings:

it is by virtue of the initial contemplation of the mind of opposition and the power of their vows that the contemplative cause is spontaneously brought into accord with the capacities of those to be trained. Why is this so? The following passage provides the explanation.
Initially, one contemplates [the phenomena] as being provisionally established through causes and conditions, waiting for the appropriate time before they can be termed "conforming" (*anuloma*).

How much more so when, below this, one uses the cause to illustrate the fruit—since characters such as *A* are universal characteristics that constitute the contemplation of entering the provisional, they can universally employ the gate of the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*), the stainless [contemplation], and others as their practice. If this is the case, they may also be called "inconceivable provisionality" (*acintya-prajñapti*), yet...
In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), they are still termed "gradual" and the dull-witted bodhisattvas are still termed "entering the cream" (*sarpis*).

For those of sharp faculties, this is termed "entering the middle. Since entering [the path] in this assembly is termed "supreme among the supreme," there is no lack of beginning and end within that which is supreme among the supreme;
it defines the marks of attaining the Way at every stage. From the passage "If one knows [the lower stages] down to penetrating the Buddha-way," this is precisely the text [that illustrates this].
Regarding the contemplation of the mind by subduing the contrary mind: the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is not limited to specific teachings; it permeates all flavors of practice and all paths.

As for the mention of "gradual" and "sudden," this fully sets forth the beginning and end [of the teaching] so that one may know that there is nothing within the Buddha’s transformation that is not the Buddha-way.

Because these are inconceivable designations (*prajñapti*), one should know that the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) fully contain the three kinds of bodhisattva designations, as well as the inconceivability of the stages (*bhūmi*) and abodes (*vihāra*).

By way of provisional interpretation, this also encompasses the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, yet it is based solely on the teachings of the Exoteric Vehicle (*vyākaraṇa-dharma*) and does not derive from the perspective of emptiness;
therefore, one cannot discuss this matter therein. Now, taking those who commit the most heinous acts as the foremost, they represent the ultimate limit of evil.

The reason for fully demonstrating these two types of characteristics is that if only the possibility of repentance were shown, people might claim that the retribution for crimes such as patricide has no fruit.

If one were to fear that by merely not repenting, people would say that sin cannot be extinguished, these two [stages] are established according to their faculties in order to eliminate such heterodox views and to give rise to the two kinds of goodness.
Regarding "I receive" and so forth, there are two meanings; here we follow the internal reality, which is clearly and certainly not losing the bliss of the *Śūraṅgama*.
How could it be said to pertain solely to the Third Dhyāna? This is discussed from the perspective of its traces (*li*).

This is because he manifested the ultimate limit of shame and resistance; therefore, what is now spoken from the perspective of his provisional emergence—namely, the three dhyānas—is a statement for revealing his traces (*traces* = *jì*).

The reason this can be interpreted through the lens of "original and trace" (*běnjì*) is that among all Mahāyāna sūtras, with the exception of the secret of the Tathāgata’s long-standing originality and the statements regarding Śāriputra attaining Buddhahood, it is only in the case of Devadatta that both the sūtras and the śāstras provide the textual basis for such an exposition.

Vāsudeva is an example of this. In these passages, all the various samādhis are employed from among the twenty-five samādhis because the "King Samādhi" (Rāja-samādhi) is simply the three samādhis of the Three Truths.
Since it follows the sequential order and employs only the conventional truth (saṃvṛti), it is said that "the Buddha-dharma is not yet complete," and so forth.
The term "incomplete" (amita/apūrṇa) also applies generally to the Three Truths. [End of] Supplement.
Since this section further enters into the profound mystery (*chongxuan*), each and every phrase states "one's own practice" (*zixing*) and so forth; all subsequent phrases are likewise so.

Vasubandhu has provided a detailed explanation in the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes), and the details regarding the elephant and other metaphors are as found in the *Zhiguan Ji* (Record of the Meditation and Contemplation).

Regarding the verse from the *Qing Guanyin Jing* (Sutra on Invoking Avalokiteśvara) cited in the *Zhiguan*, the phrase "this tenfold [practice] and so forth" (*ci shi duo you deng zhe*) refers to the fact that since it does not distinguish them individually, they are treated as a majority.
Generally speaking, according to this principle, breaking the precepts definitely belongs to the paths of action (*karmapatha*);

as for the others, they are for the most part afflictions (*kleśa*), which is why it says "for the most part. Thus we know that if they arise internally, they belong to the afflictions; those that cannot be restrained mostly belong to the paths of action.
As for "receiving various sensations while having nothing to receive," although this refers to the ten obscurations (*āvaraṇa*), it constitutes each of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Regarding those such as Śāriputra and Subhūti, whose obscurations were all penetrated to the center, one should know that their being subjected to censure or receiving empowerment was merely a manifestation of the traces (*vyañjana*) to demonstrate the sequence of practice;
here, however, we speak according to the fundamental reality (*mūla*), saying they did not receive [censure] and so forth.

As for the statement "demonstrating entry until receiving the four continents," the sutra does not list four names; these should be established according to the meaning. Why? If one follows the example of the lowly and the ugly...

The Master Lou’s words mostly concern the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa—such as the aged, the sick, and wives and concubines—and do not apply to the other three continents. Furthermore, the northern continent (Uttarakuru) should also be excluded from the category of the "sick.
However, the term "dull-witted" (*nēḍa*) can indeed apply to all four continents; therefore, it is appropriate to speak generally of the "four continents under heaven" (*caturdvīpaka*).

As for the absence of *asuras* and the "six heavens of desire" (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara*) in the sutra, one may understand that the inclusion or exclusion of *asuras* varies according to the context. Alternatively, the mention of the six heavens of desire may serve as a general illustration.
Therefore, the sequence in the abbreviated text is briefly presented as follows: the six desires are severed regarding their causes and conditions.

As for the four teachings, because the causal stages of the Distinct and Complete [teachings] still belong to the various realms of existence and are not yet purely pure, they sever [delusions] in common with all [stages].

Regarding those who clarify that "non-path" refers to everything except the Perfect Wonderful Enlightenment, the matter is too proximate; here we clarify that even when only one grade of ignorance remains, it is still [unextinguished].

Because these are not the Way, they are set aside; only the Buddha has exhausted the Buddha-way. These two Great Beings further question and answer one another, which is precisely like the mutual striking of two stones.
Regarding "understanding according to the Dharma-characteristics," this means that what is not the Way is itself the Buddha-way.

To give rise to understanding through the Dharma-characteristics is still based on that teaching; only then can it be called the Tathāgata’s capacity. By relying on this contemplation, one is the Tathāgata.

Because it functions as such, it is cited to illustrate the category of "conduct" (*caryā*). Regarding the three meanings—namely, the capacity to produce, the nature of the genus, and the [eternal] character—these were already reconciled previously;

now they are further distinguished through contrast, and thus discussed again. In reality, that which is capable of producing gives rise to its own kind, and this generality (*jāti*) is eternally unchanging.
If there were no path of suffering, how could there be a single characteristic? If there were no path of karma, how could there be a rebound?

If there were no afflictions (*kleśa*), how could there be wisdom? Because even teachings that accord with skillful means (*upāya*) are termed "dissimilar," all other sūtras establish them separately.

Now, it is clarified that the principle of "similar arising" can be established; since birth must necessarily proceed until the attainment of the fruit, this is now established to collectively constitute the characteristic of transformation.
Thus, the explanation of "lineage" (*gotra*) is attached according to conventional sentiment, based upon its similarity.

I fear that people may not understand this, as they might think that the extinction of the seeds refers to a lack of their own kind; therefore, I have appended this according to the sentiments of the time to distinguish it from other teachings.

These "teachings of skillful means" do not clarify the true seeds. Thus, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that "good roots are absent in certain people," it reveals that while the unwholesome path can be extinguished, the wholesome path can be accomplished.
Furthermore, it employs this "absence" to lead into the subsequent phrase: "the good person possesses them. Moreover, regarding "wholesomeness":

If one argues that there are wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) which, upon reaching the time of their subsequent opening, are capable of becoming a contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), and therefore these causes are already called "seeds" from the very beginning;
then what prevents the statement that they have been entirely non-existent since the beginning? This refers to the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*).

Whether one speaks from the perspective of non-existence, or speaks from the perspective of the revealing cause as something manifested—if that were so, it would also be possible for the contributing cause to be non-existent. Why?

It is only for the sake of establishing the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) that the conditions are explained through the aspect of existence (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*), and the causes are explained provisionally through the aspect of concealment (*saṃvṛti-lakṣaṇa*).

If there were no eight consciousnesses, there would be neither birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor nirvāṇa; because the eighth is the ripening (*vipāka*) consciousness, it is called "birth-and-death," yet the very essence of this birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the essential nature of this consciousness contains both of these. If that is so, then the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] are likewise [nirvāṇa].
Question: Why can the consciousness of birth and death not be called *nirvāṇa* itself? Answer: If one considers it in a general sense, this meaning is indeed possible.

However, according to the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages), when the seventh consciousness is severed and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the six consciousnesses are extinguished, this refers to the fact that the seventh consciousness is capable of grasping the pure aspects within the eight [consciousnesses].

As long as true cultivation has not yet manifested, these [aspects] belong to the six [consciousnesses]; therefore, in the present context, it is the cognitive obstructions within the six [consciousnesses] that are extinguished.
This clarifies that among the eight [categories], pure true cultivation must be derived from works such as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

This is because the Master Di (Kuei-chi) regards these eight as being subsumed within oneself, whereas the Master [Jizang] regards them as being "other"; thus, they are refuted by the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

Having used the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* to refute the body, consciousness, afflictions, unwholesome states, and so forth, this sutra then reveals the terminology of the "three paths" of the present scripture—namely, the body and the rest.

Within this body, the six or seven factors that naturally possess the nature of retribution all belong to the path of suffering; those that give rise to afflictions belong to the afflictions themselves;

and the accomplishment of karmic bonds belongs to the unwholesome. These three are thus the three causes. Why then do you needlessly dispute these three natures as being neither sequential nor simultaneous?

How could they possibly wait until the attainment of the fruit to become such? It is simply that at the time of the three paths, they are inherently neither vertical nor horizontal. How could it be otherwise?
Regarding the letter *i* (伊): whether vertical or horizontal, the fruit is not inherently existent within the principle of nature (*li*).

Since the *i* represents a profound contemplation of where the three paths reside—and as they reside within a single thought-moment, they cannot be [separated into] vertical or horizontal—it is known that both cause and effect are like the letter *i*.
The three gates are distinct: the gate of suffering, the universal gate, and the particular gate. These will be presented one by one in sequence below; first, regarding the gate of suffering:

Regarding the clarification of the meaning of the "gates": the three paths follow one another and are all subsumed under suffering. Since the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) states that each [gate] consists of three, they correspond to the fundamental gate of suffering;
thus, there are the three paths of transcending thought (*virati-manasikāra*). Furthermore, these are distinct and cannot be treated as merely general. First, regarding "the body and so forth":

the preceding text has already identified the body as the path of suffering, which is the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*); the sixth is the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), and the seventh is the completing cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*).

Because they are now combined once more to constitute the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*), and because the body as a seed is capable of producing merit and wisdom—these three points can be understood in contrast to the [previous] three.
I fear that this passage from the *Sūtra* might still be clung to as provisional; it is merely shown with diligence.
This is explained in detail in the *Zhiguan ji* and the *Fahua shu* within the section on the six dharmas being neither identical nor separate, which states: "It is like a person with cataracts..."
The mention of "the eye and so forth" is a metaphor applied to the Two Vehicles based on their direction, sphere, and form;

it also means that these are the seeds of the three Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as was already clarified in the previous discussion of the path of suffering. Although craving belongs to the afflictions, since it relies upon the body and depends upon karma, it likewise possesses these three [aspects].
How could one destroy delusion by contemplating delusion alone? One must necessarily contemplate the delusion together with its basis and...

This is because delusion arises from karma and suffering. Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are thus, among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), the two hindrances of torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are likewise of the nature of retribution (*vipāka-dharma*);
because they are mutually associated, they are also identical to suffering. Therefore, it is necessary to speak of all three.

If one were to exclude the "grasping at self" (*ātma-grāha*), they would be listed separately as three; however, since the notion of a self is common to all, they simply constitute three. If one were to exclude the "emergence of self," [the same logic would apply].

The meaning of the "Gate of Equal Discrimination" (*samavikalpa-mukha*), which is established through the three pervasions, clarifies that because one erroneously calculates the aggregates (*skandhas*), they are collectively attributed to the body, permanence, and so forth.

Thus, within the gate of suffering (*duḥkha-mukha*) and the path of suffering, the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) are extracted as separate gates; these are the specific aspects of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Because one adds the capacity for contemplative observation, they are called "foundations" (*upasthāna*) when they arise from their respective aspects. Furthermore, from the arising of these aspects, the body and so forth are again [established].

Because [the sūtra] employs names such as "right effort," "the bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), and even "the factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), one should know that the passages concerning the body and so forth also transition into the six subsequent gates.

All of these should be explained through the lens of "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). One should further understand that the four inversions are not the path, whereas the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment give rise to the Buddha-way;
they are able to produce the root and so forth. Question: It is said that they can indeed obscure meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the characteristics of meditative concentration.

Question: If the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are contrary [to dhyāna], where does the arising of [the meditative state] occur? Answer: If one refers to the Hīnayāna, the hindrances are indeed contrary [to it].

However, according to the Mahāyāna teaching, one penetrates the hindrances and thereby accomplishes concentration; thus, according to the Mahāyāna teaching, it is called "arising" (*samutthāna*). Question: If that is so, why does it arise specifically from the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*)? Answer:

Because both phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*tattva*) are clearly illuminated, it arises concurrently with them. Alternatively, perhaps it was originally intended that the phenomenal aspect assists the [principle].

This does not hinder either the specific or the general [classification], because the three paths are also fully present within the *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances). Thus, it is explained generally that the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra speaks of ten kinds of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Regarding the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), "station" (*sthiti*) refers to that which is dwelt in, while "dwelling" (*sthātṛ*) refers to that which dwells.

According to Master Kumārajīva, they exist only within the realm of suffering (*duḥkha-dhātu*); yet, in whatever station one dwells, the three paths are complete, thereby also constituting the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Three.

The mutual agreement of the Path regarding the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) holds that while one delights in dwelling in the state of having no seeds through the crushing [of defilements], though it is said that one does not delight [in this], in principle, the conditions for the arising of wholesome states are not entirely absent.
For the time being, from the perspective of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), these are universally taken as objects of contemplation; how could any such seed fail to become a cause?

As for the statement "evil gives rise to the wholesome" and so forth, this is cited to serve as an illustrative analogy for the principle that all great evils can be transformed. Since this is already established...
It should be understood that when [the three types of non-protection] are transformed into the "well-born" (sujāta), they constitute the essence of non-protection (*anārakṣa*).

Just as moist soil can produce dry soil, and once it has become dry soil, it immediately becomes bricks and tiles—thereby knowing that moist soil is the very substance of the bricks and tiles—so too, those who give rise to the three kinds of *dharmakāya* may all be designated as possessing the *dharmakāya*. This is because, just as the three [poisons] exist within suffering, so it is here.
Regarding the passage "planting seeds in emptiness" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and so forth: "emptiness" refers to being without fertilizer; it does not mean the great void.
Regarding "compassion and pity conforming to one another": the female nature is gentle and does not contend with things; thus, compassion and pity can easily be gathered together.

As for "that which resembles and that which is real": resembling is the virtuous, while real is the sage. This applies to the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*bhedavāda* and *pariniṣpanna-yāna*) and so forth; however, one must first necessarily...

Having completed the explanation by means of the first two teachings, we shall next proceed according to the latter two. Regarding the first two teachings, they merely sever the afflictions within the realm (*dhātu*);

however, if one relies on the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagdeśanā*), the removal of both *dṛṣṭi-heya* (afflictions abandoned through vision) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation) within and outside the realm all possesses a sequence of before and after, which can easily be inferred from one another.

In the case of the Bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*), although they share the same essence (*tathatā*), the principle is not that there is no sequence; even when entering the stages within the Separate Teaching, one still distinguishes between the paths of vision and cultivation.

Regarding the distinction between the initial and the final stages, in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), from beginning to end there is no duality; thus, one cannot divide it into the differences between the stages of seeing (darśana) and cultivation (bhāvanā).
Furthermore, within the realm of desire, the stage where views are exhausted is termed "purity of vision" (dṛṣṭi-viśuddhi) and "purity beyond doubt" (kāṅkṣā-viśuddhi);

the stage where the limits of thought are exhausted is termed "purity of discernment" (vijñapti-viśuddhi) and "purity of practice" (pratipatti-viśuddhi). As for *nirvāṇa*, it must be pointed to as the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood. If, regarding...

Regarding the establishment of the seven purities (*sapta-viśuddhi*) within the true stages (*bhūmi*): though they are not inherently distinct, they are divided into seven purities based on the analogy of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).

It can be seen that when it says "the Bodhisattva is in the causal stage," etc., this is because among the seven purities there is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), which is not yet the ultimate fruit.
Thus, even while a Bodhisattva cultivates the causes for no-more-learning, it may still be termed "Nirvana. Furthermore, one further cultivates the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*).
"To remove defilements" means to sever all obstacles to the dhyānas, including ignorance, as well as to cultivate the nine kinds of great dhyānas and so forth;
it may also be said that within all dhyānas, ignorance is entirely eliminated.

In the twenty-sixth fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra*, the third line of the first four-line verse distinguishes the Two Vehicles; this intention precisely accords with the meaning of the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings.

Alternatively, it may be said that the meaning of the Two Vehicles in the Shared Teaching (*tōngjiào*) is identical to that of the Tripitaka, while those in the stages prior to the Grounds in the Distinct Teaching (*biéjiào*) are termed "partial" (*piān*).

Regarding the "gate," if the first stage (*bhūmi*) is termed "entering the perfect principle" (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*), it differs from what follows; thus, it is not the same as the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*).

Some say that the stages prior to the path of teaching (*śikṣāmārga*) are not yet the entry into the Perfect [Teaching], and are only called the "perfect principle" when spoken of from the perspective of realization (*adhigama*). The fourth set of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) serves to distinguish this from the third set of four propositions.
Although the preceding [third set] contrasts principle and teaching to establish the gate, it remains unknown which specific teaching’s doctrine and principle are being referred to.

One must distinguish [the true] from the false: immediately departing from subject and object, the perfect and the distinct further correspond to the Treasuries (pitaka) to reveal the sequence of the preceding principles and teachings.

The five and four phrases are precisely for the purpose of distinguishing the preceding four sets of four phrases; although the preceding [distinctions] all proceed from the Dharma and analyze it in relation to the Principle (li), they have not yet discussed "entering.
Now, regarding silence and non-silence, this gate is established again from the perspective of practice to re-examine the previous four. As for the sixth set of four phrases:
In the previous [section], the Perfect Teaching was elucidated by contrasting the person of causes with the person of fruits; now, it should further be distinguished by means of two teachings.

Regarding the seventh set of four propositions, gain and loss are differentiated based on attainment and failure, manifesting that all preceding cases involve attainment, whereas this present case involves a trace of failure.

Regarding the eighth set of four propositions, the contrast between the present and the past is discussed in terms of inclusion and exclusion, or attainment and non-attainment, based upon the teachings of the single lifetime of the Buddha.
Regarding these characteristics, within the first seven sets of four phrases, the past and present are discussed together to evaluate gain and loss;

this is also done by contrasting the partial (*prādeśika*) and the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*), where only the fourth gate is perfect and constitutes "gain. Subsequently, the nine sets of four phrases distinguish the great from the small through the contrast of the fruit and its relative;
here, the first phrase refers to the small fruit, while the latter three refer to the great contemplation, which is also called the "Great Cause" (*mahāhetu*). This is according to the Dharma.

The Fourteenth Section on the *Huaxiangdailun* (Treatise on the Mutual Expectation of the Flowers), concerning the fourth phrase: Although this is purely based on the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*), and although there are many gates, the intent lies in contemplation;
therefore, the gate of contemplation is explained last. Regarding "the two" and "the non-two": as in the ten gates mentioned above, one distinguishes between entering and not entering.
Those who enter are categorized as either partial or perfect. The perfect is the non-two, while the partial is the two. This non-two is precisely what is intended here.

Regarding the two types of entry, they are indeterminate—being either deviant or correct, small or great, pertaining only to phenomena (*dharma*) or only to principle (*tattva*), or distinguishing only a single meaning—and they may either exist or not exist.

As will be fully distinguished below, one should know that these are excluded in order to distinguish them from the "non-entry" [into the path]. If one attains entry, one does not fall into any of these errors;
thus, it is simply the Dharma of equality. As for the terms "non-duality" (*advaya*) and "gate" (*mukha*), they are merely... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

Although there are differences in how a single dharma is established—being established as a "dharma" based on its locus and named based on its function—the essence of the dharma is without distinction;
therefore, it is said to be "non-dual. Regarding this, while the various gates may be dual, they are non-dual when both extremes are abandoned.

To say that one "abandons attachment to the middle" means that the principle of the Middle Way is designated as a "gate" to reveal that the teaching itself is the principle to be entered. (The *Lotus Sūtra*)
Regarding the phrase "the gate of wisdom," etc.: the principle itself is the gate; because the wisdom within this gate accords with that principle, it is difficult [to express].
Thus, the text borrows the term "opening" (kai) to manifest this difficulty; it is also a designation for the mutual correspondence between the object and the wisdom.

As for the analogy "like a person knowing that house," etc., this refers to the stage prior to abiding (zhùqián), where knowing the perfection serves as a metaphor to reveal that entering the stage of true abiding (zhùfēnzhēn) is called "entry" (rù). Furthermore:
The proponent further clarifies the function of the fruit; thus it is said that "the progressive discourse" is fully as explained in the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation).
This indicates that what is contained herein is exactly as previously interpreted—namely, the thirty-three heavens, the fourteen *prajñās*, and the forty-two letters.

As for the phrase "if one were to treat each as a separate gate," this refers back to the preceding section where, in response to Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, the thirty-two individuals were categorized according to the same principle.
The section on the Distinct Teaching is concluded; now, through further questions and answers, it is revealed that the Perfect [Teaching] cannot be exclusively categorized as the Distinct Teaching.

If one gate encompasses all thirty-two gates, then the same applies to all gates. Thus, regarding the ultimate non-binding nature of the provisional and the real, as discussed in the *Visiting the Sick* chapter in the contrast between wisdom and skillful means regarding bondage and liberation, what is here called "sovereignty" refers precisely to these two functions; "wisdom" is the real wisdom.
Therefore it is said that the two wisdoms consist of the sovereign wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*) and the unconditioned wisdom of reality (*tattva-prajñā*).

This is why, regarding the initial mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*), there is extensive analysis and selection; for this [text] stands at the head of all bodhisattvas. All subsequent major themes must be understood according to this principle.

Thus, the characteristics of the various explanations below are all abbreviated. As for the five planets and twenty-eight lunar mansions, they are fully explained as in the *Zhi guan ji* (Record of the Meditation Manual).

Regarding "these movements of thought" and so forth: because thought moves, the object moves; now, however, we simply take the unmoving mind as a general counterpoint to the moving object, and thus the objects and wisdom of the three teachings are termed "dual," whereas only the object of the Perfect Teaching (the *yuanjiao*) is termed "non-dual" and "without movement of thought.
"The one with good eyes" refers to the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*); this is the partial attainment of the World-Honored One’s eye of wisdom.

Regarding the "one characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and "characteristicless" (*alakṣaṇa*): both the three interpretations of the Mahāyāna and the single interpretation of the Hīnayāna schools do not differentiate between the depths of "one characteristic" and "characteristicless.
Furthermore, if one were to wait for the clarification of "one" and "non-existence," it would be unnecessary. Now, taking the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) and other texts as authority:

it is not that "one" is different [from non-existence], nor is it that "one" is non-existence; rather, it is precisely when this "one" and "non-existence" are neither [separate] nor identical that they are called "non-duality" (*advaya*).
Next, as below, first take one to refute number; then, with "one-characteristic" and "no-characteristic," both refute oneness.
To call it "non-dual" (advaya) is merely a designation. Furthermore, there are three dharmas which open up the mind to make four; this phrasing is somewhat abbreviated and should rather say:

"furthermore, there are three dharmas—form and the mental concomitants—and furthermore, there are four dharmas which open up the mind to make three. Thus, the King and the mental concomitants are the same.
Time and form constitute four; furthermore, there are five dharmas: opening the mind into four and pairing them with form as five.

This is merely the provisional teaching of the Āgamas, which opens and closes the categories of form and mind to explain the one and the many, temporarily manifesting their characteristics for the sake of illustration rather than as a permanent application.

If one does not descend [to this level], it correctly clarifies that within the phenomena of contemplation, the wondrous is the provisional [aspect] of the same essence, while the inconceivable is the real.

Regarding the identity of provisional and ultimate principles, the Bodhisattva mind and the Śrāvaka mind—this refers to the two types of Bodhisattvas in contrast to the two types of vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) within the two teachings.
As for Puṣya, he first understood the dissolution [of these distinctions]; hereafter follows the refutation of the old [interpretations]. Now, taking up the following, the correct explanation begins.

Within the "Lion’s Roar," first, the similarities and differences are distinguished by means of two names from the worldly perspective; if one takes up the following, it refutes the old [views], and now, reaching the section below, the correct explanation proceeds.

Because the lion-like mind is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is "vigorous. Regarding the phrase "under the term 'tainted'": first, he generally presents the characteristics of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted;

then, under the heading "the term 'tainted'," he provides the formal explanation. Within the explanation of "pure understanding" (*viśuddha-adhimukti*), he first distinguishes the names and their referents (*nāma* and *vastu*). His intention is this:

although the names "tainted" and "untainted" were already established in the preceding text, he now further establishes the names "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) because the categories (*mukha*) differ; therefore, he establishes them once again.

Regarding the statement, "The conditioned is opposed to the three unconditioned; now, as for 'transcending all numbers' and so forth": within the conditioned, one counts [the categories] and opposes them to the numbers within the three unconditioned;
taking cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as one, they are termed "two. If those numbers and the cessation of numbers do not exist, then they are "non-dual" (*advaya*).
This is the primary intent of the passage from the beginning of the *Nārāyaṇa-parivarta* down to the end, which correctly clarifies the meaning as it appears in the text.

Because one does not abandon [the view] after having already perceived the Middle Way, it is called "presently seeing. From "delusion is ignorance" up to "old age and death," this fully indicates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
This current contemplation is established by means of the intent of the Sūtra. If this current contemplation does not exhaustively [realize] emptiness, it is the emptiness of the Middle Way.
From the words "not exhaustive" (*a-kṣaya*) downward, the emptiness within the Middle is explained; this is named "non-exhaustion. This exhaustion is not...
"Exhaustion is neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion; 'universally maintaining' (pǔshǒu) leads to the eight forms of self-mastery.

Furthermore, regarding the two names "self" and "non-self," both are situated within the middle way of the *dharmatā*; therefore, they must be cited to prevent the error of assuming that identical names imply identical meanings.
Thus, they are explained by showing that while the names are the same, their meanings differ. In the *Vidyutdeva-sūtra*, it is clarified that ignorance (*avidyā*) and [wisdom] constitute these two.
This is because ignorance within the realm is not itself non-ignorance; it is only in relation to the clarity within the realm that they are treated as two.
Ignorance is itself clarity—this is the correct explanation of their characteristics, namely, the ignorance of mutual identity (*paraspara-amśa*).

Since ignorance is itself clarity, even the essence of ignorance is inherently non-dual, let alone its relationship to clarity; therefore, it is said that "Buddha-nature is itself clarity. Furthermore, there are three kinds of clarity.

The term "seed" (*bīja*) is used here as a general illustration. In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (or *Xǐjiàn jīng*), it first refutes the crude [view] and then, in the following section, provides the formal explanation:
that which exists like an illusion is precisely emptiness; that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) tend toward emptiness means that non-emptiness is itself true emptiness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the four kinds of seeds within the "characteristics of clarity," it likewise first establishes the four kinds and so forth, up to the formal explanation of non-duality (*advaya*). As for the mention of "internal and external":

"That all are empty is the essence of emptiness" refers precisely to the emptiness of the Middle Way; this can be understood through the inexhaustible meaning of the subtle intent as explained previously.

Regarding the name "profound wisdom" (*gambhīra-prajñā*), it is not explained in the text because it is the wisdom that perceives the bottomless foundation. Thus, it is called "profound," for its foundation is the reality-limit (*bhūtatathatā*).
In the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the explanation of the names of the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) states: "These are the three untainted [faculties] of the Mahāyāna."

The faculty of outflows (*āsrava-indriya*) arises from the reality-mark of quiescence (*śamatha-lakṣaṇa*). When the object and the wisdom correspond, they are in harmony; when they do not correspond, they are not in harmony.

Since the Three Jewels are explained here in terms of the object and the wisdom, it is said that when the objective dharma and the Buddha-wisdom correspond, the object also corresponds to the wisdom, and is thus called "corresponding.
To be in accord with principle means that the wisdom accords with the principle, which is precisely as previously established in relation to the principle.

Since this principle applies to the meaning of the Three Jewels of Wisdom, it likewise applies to all phenomena; there are no phenomena that are not the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the single essence of the Three Jewels.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (The Flower Ornament Scripture) regarding the non-obstruction of mind:
"To say that nirvāṇa is form, and emptiness is form—this emptiness is also the emptiness of the Middle Way. Within this Middle Way, all forms and emptinesses are fully present. Thus, it is so.
Furthermore, regarding "supreme goodness," form and mind constitute the duality. In the emptiness entered by the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle, there is still the perception of duality;

yet within the true reality (*dharmatā*), one does not perceive even a single dharma among all phenomena—how then could one distinguish between form and mind? Therefore, it is called "non-dual. Regarding the explanation of "immovability" (*akopya*) within the field of merit:
this explains that there is both progression and regression. Initially, all four *dhyānas* are termed "immovable"; subsequently, [it refers specifically to] the fourth.
Dhyāna and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) are termed "immovable" (*aniñjya*); however, what is understood here [by others] is merely that which has been explained above.

The immovability clarified here belongs solely to merit (*puṇya*), as all such [merit] is with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and therefore remains subject to movement. Only when contrasted with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state of ultimate reality is it termed "immovable.
As the Sūtra says, "From me arise the two," the intent is to clarify the destruction of the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) within non-self (*anātman*).

Therefore it is said that the arising of duality occurs because one has not yet attained realization of the nature of the self; thus, one gives rise to duality. De-zang (Guṇagañja), Yue-shang (Candrottara), Yin-shou (Mudrāhasta), and Bing-kě-jian-zhu-ding (Samantadarśinamukuṭamaṇi) are all visible;
as for the name "Juzhi" (Maṇimakuṭa), it is not explained in the text. For example, the bright jewel atop the head of a Wheel-Turning King is called "Juzhi" because this jewel resides upon his crown.
In the *Leshi* (Sukhāvatīvyūha), it says: "If spoken according to the Separate Teaching (Biaojiao), the correct contemplation of the Middle Way is wisdom."

The "Eye" (cakṣus) refers to that which is reached through distant aspiration among the ten abodes (*bhūmi*). From the ten practices (*caryā*) onward, one emerges from emptiness into the provisional; therefore, it is said to "illuminate the two truths.
Because it is viewed from the side of the provisional, it is called the "Dharma-eye" (*dharmacakṣus*). When the three truths are observed together, one enters the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

This is also a provisional correspondence to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), for the previous section has already determined that these various bodhisattvas belong to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*); thus, [this classification] cannot be applied here.
This explanation belongs to the interpretation of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). This, too, is merely a provisional judgment following the literal text.
If one speaks from a remote perspective regarding the thirty-two individuals, that which they enter is likewise ineffable.

For one who has attained the meaning, since it was previously judged that each of the thirty-two individuals interpenetrates one another, this constitutes the principle of the Perfect Teaching; therefore, within this present context, one may proceed in this manner.
The explanation that "the gate of the ineffable is also like this" means that each of the four gates— Distinct, Complete, and so forth— possesses its own fifth gate of the ineffable;
because they are ineffable, and because they are ineffable, these gates are also universally pervasive and encompass all, yet they specifically belong to the Complete Gate.
In the twenty-seventh fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-vyākhyā*:

Regarding bodhisattvas who remain in secular life and are not subsumed within the ranks of the monastic community—if one does not separately establish the three vehicles of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* (Zang and Tong) as being fully endowed with the precepts, this is as analyzed in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra).
If there is merely a strict adherence to the precepts without the vehicle (*yāna*), it is clear that there is no Mahāyāna, which serves to manifest purity.
Regarding the statement that "one who has severed the fetters of the three realms through what was to be done does not sever them all simultaneously," this means they should be removed;

since they have already been removed, it says "seven days. As for using the preceding seven days as the preparatory stage (*upāya*), this takes the aforementioned textual explanation of the seven days and applies it as the preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*) within the context of intellectual understanding;
thus, while the names differ, the meaning is the same, as described here in relation to what preceded.
To speak of distinct names is called "difference," yet their great purport does not differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s threefold exposition of the provisional; they are no different.
If one were to take the Abhidharma up to the perfect teaching of the Mahāyāna as referring to all dharmas, how could one use this Abhidharma to challenge the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
One must know with certainty that these are teachings of incomplete realization and are definitely not to be relied upon. Furthermore, if the masters of the Abhidharma were to hear this now...

Is it not the case that one would clap one's hands at such a statement? For those who take the manifestation of radiance as their task to become Buddhas, even in this land radiance is still used as the primary means;

how much more so in other lands where radiance is employed exclusively? Within the Hīnayāna, some say that "light reaching and touching" means it touches only after it has reached [the object], while "reaching without touching" means it neither reaches nor touches. Even if it were not the case of "not reaching," it would still not be beneficial.

Just as a conjured person encounters sense organs and objects, so too it is with the Bodhisattva; therefore, that which belongs to the ten similes of arising—such as the senses, dreams, and illusions—is likewise entirely like space.
Furthermore, since these ten similes fundamentally illustrate space, even "insects" (where *kūn* is a general term for insects and also means "multitude") are included.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the woman refers to Huixumi, who possessed both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the record that leads ordinary people to fall into this state, it is said in general that the characteristics of most worldly people are such;
how could [the Buddha] intentionally cause them to fall? This woman was solely for the sake of benefit; thus she is called a supramundane Brahmin, who is none other than Jvalanāmukha (Shengre).
This is detailed as found in the *Mohe Zhiguan* and its commentary, the *Shiqian*. As for "this body and land" and so forth, since the "land" can already serve as an explanation.

The body can be used to explain the land. If it refers to those who transform others and so forth, or where the provisional is said to be the real, this refers to the three kinds of truth in the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings.
Or, if the real is said to be the provisional, this includes the Middle Way and enters into the True.

These, when contrasted with the Perfect (*Yuan*), are also called "transforming others"; therefore, it is said that based on this, one distinguishes between the conceivable and the inconceivable. This is the inconceivable.

This refers to the ultimate and conventional truths within the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) and the two entrances [of the Shared Teaching]. As for the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), the Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao), and so forth:
the Distinct Teaching at times belongs to benefiting others (parārtha) and at times may also serve as one's own practice (svārtha); it is also termed "benefiting both self and others.

It is called "opening" because the Middle Way is taken as the ultimate (paramārtha-satya), hence it is said "to open. It is called "conventional" because the ultimate and conventional are treated as the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya). Thus it is said:
This is the inclusion.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*, fascicle 28,

contains the verses on the three periods of time in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* exactly as they appear in the *Fahua shuji* (Record of the Lotus Sutra Commentary) regarding the ten inconceivable dharma-gates of the dwelling stages in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Regarding the mutual comparison and determination of the two causes—actualization and arising—from beneath "reality" (*tattva*): this is explained according to their respective portions based on the conditions for non-arising.

How could there be one who has resolved upon the bodhicitta who possesses only the condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and lacks the cause of realization (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*), or who possesses only the cause of realization and lacks the condition?
If either were present alone, they would not constitute a pair of reciprocal conditions; it is only when both realization and conditions are present that [the result] is truly accomplished.

The conditions are also like this: making offerings to the *sambhoga-kāya* (the body born of life) is called the "cause of birth. This refers to those who offer only to the Buddha’s physical form (*rūpa-kāya*) without hearing the Dharma;
or those who see the *sambhoga-kāya* but only hear the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle—these are both termed "merit" that does not lead to Bodhi.

Furthermore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it states that even down to those who are enemies of the Buddhas [are included], because they are not mentioned in the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle. Therefore...

Regarding "no birth" (*anutpāda*) within the conditions of sin and merit, those who have practiced the preliminary stages of hearing and contemplation dwell in the cultivation prior to the stage of fruition;
the merits therein are fully detailed in the *Zhi guan ji* (Record of Stopping and Contemplating). As for "Nirvāṇa and Prajñā," this refers to Nirvāṇa-liberation;

that is, they are treated as two in contrast to Prajñā, because [the former] takes the Middle Way of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its object. "Complete and Sudden" (*yuantun*) is the Perfect Teaching, while "Gradual" (*cijian*) refers to the three teachings. The three...

Those who plant the seeds of birth and death differentiate causes and conditions within the midst of transformation; those who demonstrate the hundred phrases of liberation reach the ultimate fruit only when they are fully endowed with these hundred phrases.
If one is endowed with the hundred phrases, how could it be limited to only a hundred? If one is endowed with all things, why would it be restricted solely to the fruit?

Upagupta was endowed with these [qualities], as stated in the *Zhiguan ji* (Record of Calming and Contemplation). Regarding "profound sutras," this refers to citations from the *Wuxing jing* (Sutra on Non-action).
Among these, there are those who say that desire itself is the Way; this refers to sentient beings who, from time immemorial, have been in constant motion together with these three poisons.
To encourage sentient beings to attain awakening therein, it is said that "this is the great purport of all sutras. This is entirely so.

Those who do not deeply grasp the meaning may take these three to be the ultimate reality; fearing that people might misunderstand, [the Buddha] further cites that sutra to reveal that one must deeply penetrate this.
The Dharma does not violate the precepts and so forth. This person was formerly a śrāmaṇera; this is the Upādhyāya Ānanda, and this is the Ācārya.
Regarding "two, three, four, five": "two" refers to the half-month and the full month; "three" refers to the gradual [stages] and so forth; "four" refers to the four seasons;
and regarding the "three" such as the gradual stages and so forth, one further adds the permanent abiding and nirvāṇa. "Five" refers to the five periods as usual.
Regarding the three teachings—the "heard," the "refutation," and so forth—and the two teachings and one teaching, these three are likewise the gradual and so on;
the two are the sudden and the gradual; and the one refers to the single sound which has no teaching, meaning it is beyond verbal expression.

Even when employing any of the eight teachings as appropriate, one should use all the teachings in conjunction with contemplation, mutually integrating them so that the intent remains free from stagnation.

If one enters the Way through skillful means (*upāya*) and not otherwise, how would this principle differ from that of external paths? Therefore, one must give rise to practice based upon the teachings;
the cultivation of the characteristics of teaching and practice takes awakening as its foundation.
